articles.title: America Needs a Truth Commission
articles.author: Jared O. Bell
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. A few weeks ago, during a trip to the Philippines, I made my way across congested Manila to Bantayog ng mga Bayani, the memorial in Quezon City to Filipinos who resisted Ferdinand Marcos. The Wall of Remembrance outside, inscribed with the names of those who died resisting, was overrun with grass. I asked one guard where to find the museum, then another, before finding it around a corner. The receptionist asked who I was with. I told her I was a professor and researcher. She indicated to me that there were no tours on Monday and that I’d be free to tour the museum on my own. The museum was worn, its displays far smaller than the story they told of one of the most precarious periods in Philippine history. They traced Marcos’s rise and the movement, and the bloodshed, it took to stop him. The exhibits were heartbreaking and, paradoxically, empowering. Among them was a newspaper front page from 1972. Its banner headline reads “FM DECLARES MARTIAL LAW.” Just beneath it, the paper reassures readers: “But civilian gov’t still functions; no military takeover.” Farther down: “Nation is calm; business, life go on normally.” As I moved through the rooms, I kept thinking about where my own country seemed to be headed. Life did not go on normally. Under martial law, according to Amnesty International , some 70,000 people were imprisoned, 34,000 tortured and 3,240 killed. Related: From Nuremberg to the ICC: America’s War on International Justice What stayed with me was what happened after. Filipinos drove Marcos from power in 1986. But many officials who had tortured prisoners kept their posts , and a law recognizing and compensating victims did not arrive until 2013 , 27 years later. By then, a sustained campaign to recast the era as a golden age was well underway. In 2022, Marcos’s son won the presidency in a landslide . An uprising had removed the father. It did not settle what he had done. I think one of the key lessons from the Philippines is that when a country has no way of dealing with its past, the abuses come back. Three years after that reparations law, Rodrigo Duterte became president. He allowed Marcos to be buried in the national Heroes’ Cemetery and launched a drug war that killed more than 6,000 people by the government’s own count and as many as 30,000 by the estimates of human rights groups. In 2022, Duterte’s daughter, Sara, ran alongside Marcos’s son and became vice president. Their alliance has since fallen apart . Marcos let the International Criminal Court arrest the elder Duterte, whose trial for crimes against humanity opens on Nov. 30. Even that reckoning is happening in The Hague, and only because two political families turned on each other. I have been thinking about that newspaper since voters handed Democrats control of both the House and Senate . Hakeem Jeffries promised to “bring accountability to those who have visited unprecedented corruption on this country.” I have spent more than 15 years in international development, leading governance and accountability programs in Central Asia, Africa, the Balkans, and Latin America, including at the U.S. Agency for International Development. The United States financed truth commissions from South Africa to Colombia. It has never applied those tools to itself. In 2025, to my shock, horror and disbelief, I watched that agency dismantled, and I was pushed out along with nearly all of its staff . I believed in it, regardless of its imperfections. It was a purge of “deep state” operatives, who apparently couldn’t or wouldn’t be loyal to the president or his agenda. We were treated as enemies of the American people and the government we served. Over the past two years, I have watched things happen here that I spent my career helping activists and concerned citizens fight against. In a single night in January 2025, President Trump fired 17 inspectors general . The Justice Department dropped corruption charges against allies, including New York’s then-mayor, Eric Adams , and opened investigations of opponents. A federal judge found probable cause that officials had willfully defied his order halting deportation flights. In Minneapolis, federal immigration agents killed two American citizens, Renée Good and Alex Pretti , an ICU nurse. Related: The War on “Socialism” Is Really a War on the Public Good The new majorities will be tempted to answer all of this with two years of hearings aimed at the 2028 campaign. I understand the appeal. It would also play into the “lawfare” narrative the administration has spent years building. The White House is already making that case. Days after the election, Trump called Democrats’ investigative requests “ extortion at the highest level ” and ordered the Justice Department to look into them. The White House counsel then warned Robert Garcia, the incoming Oversight Committee chairman, that aggressive oversight “ may cross the line into blatant criminality .” Garcia, for his part, had posted “ LAWYER UP ” on election night. Hearings run as a fight between two parties will only help Trump tell his story. There must be justice and accountability, in a sequenced manner. Congress should start by creating an independent truth commission by statute. Of course, it doesn’t have to be called a truth commission, and it may draw some political ire from Democrats and Republicans alike, as it may appear as retribution or an overreaction to the harms done. The House January 6 committee expired with the Congress that created it. A statutory body with subpoena power, bipartisan appointments and terms that outlast the next election could produce a full public accounting of how American institutions broke down. The closest American precedent is the 9/11 Commission . I first came to this work as a doctoral student in Morocco, whose truth commission could not compel officials to testify or publicly name perpetrators. Years later, I taught at a university in The Gambia as the country rolled out its Truth, Reconciliation and Reparations Commission after Yahya Jammeh’s long rule. Both commissions left behind a public record, something congressional hearings rarely do. President Trump will almost certainly veto such a bill. Congress should pass it anyway. A veto becomes part of the record, and the legislation will be ready in 2029. The findings should then drive institutional reform, including real protection for inspectors general and a statutory bar on the new rule stripping civil service protections from career employees. Prosecutions should be left to the courts, without political interference. Deciding who should be barred from public office is the hardest part, and it should come last. That decision has to rest on what a person did and what a court has proven, rather than on which party they belong to. The Philippines let torturers keep their jobs, and it is still living with the consequences. Iraq went the other way, and its de-Baathification turned into a purge of anyone tied to the old ruling party. Related: Mr. Secretary, What America Needs Is an Independent Press, Not an Actual Patriotic Press I understand why many Americans will hear “accountability” as “retribution.” That is why the order matters. A truth process that comes first, run by an independent body, is the strongest protection against a cycle of partisan revenge. And every reform described here would bind a future Democratic president just as tightly as this one. “Nation is calm; business, life go on normally.” In 1972, that headline was meant to reassure Filipinos. When I read it in that museum, it felt like a warning. I spent years writing about and researching how other countries reckon with their pasts. If the U.S. is the society dedicated to the rule of law that we claim to be, we should be making the case for our own reckoning at home. PeaceVoice

articles.title: Fight Facing the New Congress
articles.author: Roxanne D. Brown
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. We sent a clear message on Election Day about what we want from the next Congress—affordability, accountability, and an economy that works for all. We’re disgusted with empty promises from a government that lavishes ever more on the do-nothing rich while working families fall further into the margins. We’ve had it with CEOs pocketing obscene sums while doling out scraps to everyone else and with billionaires frittering away huge sums to divide us. But tens of millions of working people just took back the wheel. We demonstrated how powerful we are when we come together. We showed that the future belongs to us , not to the 1 percent. And make no mistake, the path forward means making it easier for workers to form unions so we can continue to grow collective power and keep the uber-rich from siphoning away every good thing. Americans feel more disillusioned about the economy at present than they did during the depths of the pandemic. We’ve lost confidence in the nation’s institutions and see the country turning into something we no longer recognize. Related: Trump’s Canada Tariffs Put American Steel Jobs at Risk Yet growing numbers support unions like the United Steelworkers (USW) and want us to wield greater influence in American life. That’s because we’re committed, the way nobody else is, to building that economy for all. We force corporations to fork over a fair share, treat everyone equitably, and afford each person a voice. There’s no end to the affordability crisis—no strong middle class nor vibrant democracy, either—without more union workers. By banding together, workers win fair wages, affordable healthcare, safe working conditions, retirement security, and a seat at the table. Union workers, on average, make significantly higher wages and better benefits than nonunion peers. In turn, good union contracts enable us to double down on our communities. We support civic groups, volunteer our time, support local businesses, and advocate for good government, as we did leading up to the November 3 election. We’re the key to weathering inflation, surviving the next pandemic, and sustaining our freedom. Unlike working people, the rich and their cronies care only about themselves. Related: America’s Dead-End Economy Bad for Everyone For example, CEOs and shareholders oppose legislation to end employer interference in union elections, better safeguard union activists, and impose real penalties on violators. These same moneyed interests resist a bill that would prevent employers from dragging their feet when newly unionized workers come to the table to bargain for the fair contracts they deserve. Corporations even stonewall measures to protect miners from silica exposure and protect healthcare workers from violence on the job. This greed has real consequences. Millions of workers want to join unions but fall short every year because of employer harassment and retaliation. Many have to work multiple bad jobs instead of one good one. Others forgo doctor’s visits because bosses skimp on benefits when there’s no union to hold their feet to the fire. Related: Want to Rebuild the Middle Class? Triple Union Membership Too many of us continue to get sick, sustain injuries, and die because of unsafe working conditions. It would be an understatement to say that we just gave the new Congress a mandate to change all of this. We defied history and beat the odds. We overcame a gerrymandering scheme, voter suppression, billion-dollar misinformation campaigns, intimidation, fearmongering, and other cheating to take a stand. We valued people over money. We won the day. Now it’s time to right the country. Produced by the Independent Media Institute .

articles.title: Single-Payer Healthcare Deadlock
articles.author: Larry Gross
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. California would seem to be the most likely state to enact a true single-payer healthcare program [SP]. After all, SP is favored by majorities, including Republicans. However, successive legislative efforts to pass CalCare, the SP plan sponsored by the California Nurses Association [CNA], have been killed by Democratic leaders before they could come to a vote. Actually, that’s not quite true: SP bills were passed by the CA legislature twice, when Republican governor Arnold Schwarzenegger promised to veto them. When Democrat Gavin Newsom, who ran on a SP platform and was supported by CNA, was elected, he made sure that no SP bill ever reached his desk. The reason for the repeated failure of SP legislation is not a mystery: the immense wealth of the health insurance complex gives them an unsurmountable advantage in determining the actions of Democratic politicians in the legislature and the governor’s office. To put it simply, when serious interests are at stake, legislators can be bribed or they can be scared. The SP forces are woefully outmatched financially, and have not yet been able to inspire the sort of public outrage that would effectively scare enough legislators. Thus, it’s not surprising that SP advocates are once again considering the option of a ballot measure that would enshrine healthcare as a right, and SP as the vehicle, in the California constitution. In 1994 CA voters defeated Proposition 186, which would have established a universal, publicly financed, single-payer health care system in California, effectively eliminating private health insurance as the principal means of paying for medical care. There were numerous reasons that effort failed, among them the timing: the Clinton health reform initiative collapsed in Congress in September 1994, just weeks before the California election. But among the major reasons the proposition failed was the enormous financial advantage of the opponents, who outspent proponents $9 million to $2.7 million. Related: Socialist Health Care Organizers Exit DSA The opposition concentrated on three arguments: higher taxes, increased government control of medical decisions, and uncertainty about the quality and availability of care under a completely reorganized system. More than 30 years later, the public is much more sophisticated about the realities of health care and certainly much more aware of the disadvantage of the profit-centered system of private health insurance, which have only become more acute with the invasion of the health sphere by private equity vultures. Any campaign to pass a SP proposition would once again have to counter the false claims that SP would cost citizens more, and would have to show business owners, as well as union members and leaders, how they would benefit by taking health insurance costs off the benefit bargaining table. But these are more achievable goals today, after decades of insurance company over-reach and greed, and with a public increasingly angered and anguished by the rising costs and diminishing benefits of private insurance. Now that the next governor will be Xavier Beccera, who has made it clear that he doesn’t support SP, there’s no point in resurrecting a doomed-to-fail legislative campaign. So what’s to prevent the advocates of SP from embarking on a ballot measure campaign? The standard answer, of course, is the enormous amount of money that would be needed, even assuming a successful grassroots campaign could be organized, with the necessary enthusiastic participation of a broad coalition of labor and community organizations. It’s the money, stupid, is the familiar refrain one hears when the topic is raised. But there might be an answer to that conversation stopper. What if there was a billionaire around who was strongly and sincerely dedicated to achieving SP healthcare in California, and was easily able to seed a ballot measure campaign with the millions needed to launch and sustain the effort ? There just might be. Tom Steyer ran in the recent gubernatorial primary on a platform that was unambiguous about his [newly acquired] support for SP: Tom knows quality health care is a right, not a privilege – and that there’s too much profit, and not enough health care, in our health care system. That’s why he’s been endorsed by the California Nurses Association , and progressive single payer health care champions like Congressman Ro Khanna and Representative Ash Kalra, the author of Cal-Care. Tom believes strongly that the only way we’ll reduce health care costs, expand coverage, and promote public health when it is under attack from the Trump administration is through a single-payer system . And he is committed to getting California there. As the largest and most powerful state, California will set an example for the rest of the United States to follow. Tom Steyer spent a reported $220 million on his unsuccessful campaign for the gubernatorial nomination, which would make spending, say, $22 million on a single-payer ballot measure a real bargain. This is the moment for the advocates of SP in California, including the California Nurses Association, to challenge Tom Steyer to put his money where his campaign platform was, and to provide the necessary funding to launch a broad-based coalition to put a true SP measure on the ballot in 2028.

articles.title: War Budget Is a Path to Spiritual Death
articles.author: Ryan Wentz
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. In the coming weeks, Congress will be voting on Trump’s proposed $1.5 trillion war budget, double the number it was under Biden, which, of course, was already far too high. If passed, the U.S. military budget will be larger than the military budgets of the next 34 countries combined. Thirty-four countries combined. What’s more, while the Pentagon has been audited eight times, not once has it passed. In 1967, Martin Luther King Jr. declared: “A nation that continues year after year to spend more money on military defense than on programs of social uplift is approaching spiritual death.” Think about what we should be spending money on: programs of social uplift — programs like Medicare for All, universal childcare, and tuition-free college. We desperately need to address the climate crisis, improve public transportation, and raise the minimum wage. Related: The Authoritarian Awareness “Sweet 16” Glossary Test According to the National Priorities Project, last year, our $1.07 trillion war budget could have funded: 122.47 million public housing units or 10.06 million livable wage jobs for a single parent with two children or 471.98 million people receiving SNAP benefits or 11.4 million elementary school teachers or 28.69 million borrowers receiving federal student loan forgiveness or 64.19 million people receiving paid parental leave or 125.15 million people receiving Medicaid or 2.02 billion households with solar electricity. The list goes on. The justification for this massive budget, and for wars and imperialism in general, is a pile of lies. One outrageous lie after another — so many of them that the warmongers in Washington have seemingly lost track of them. A couple of days ago, journalist Rania Khalek, who was in the halls of Congress with Medea Benjamin and dozens of CODEPINK organizers from around the country, asked Representative Joe Wilson if he’d continue to support funding the Iran war despite its unpopularity. The representative’s answer? “I oppose terrorists who murder babies, putting them in microwaves.” This simply never happened. America’s best and brightest, folks. Several years ago, then-Secretary of State and ex-CIA Director Mike Pompeo admitted: “I was the CIA director. We lied, we cheated, we stole. It was like we had entire training courses. It reminds you of the glory of the American experiment.” Yes, he actually said that — and he wasn’t wrong. That’s what the US empire does: the White House, Congress, the corporate media, the CIA, and the Pentagon. Lies, lies, and more lies. They lie about Iran and boom: the US bombs an Iranian elementary school and kills roughly 160 schoolchildren and staff. They lie about Venezuela and boom: the US kidnaps Venezuela’s president and first lady and steals its oil. They lie about drug trafficking and boom: the US wages a deadly bombing campaign against fishermen in the Caribbean and the Pacific. They lie about Cuba and boom: the US blocks fuel from reaching the island, strangling the Cuban people. They lie about Gaza and boom: genocide. Contrary to popular American mythology, we don’t promote human rights and spread democracy abroad. We kill people, overthrow governments, starve entire populations, arm genocidal apartheid regimes and absolute monarchies, threaten international institutions, and destroy ecosystems. Dr. King was right: the US empire is a project of spiritual, physical, and economic death. Our movement, however, fights for truth, meaning we fight for life. We know a better world is possible. We see the children of Gaza, Iran, and Cuba as our own. We understand that diplomacy, not war, is the way to build peace. We seek to be good neighbors, not only in the Western Hemisphere, but all across the globe. We want clean air and water, safety, and dignity for all. That’s why we must mobilize to stop this $1.5 trillion war budget. Because we love and value life — here in Los Angeles, in Rafah, in Tehran, in Havana, and beyond. Commit to the struggle. Dare to imagine something beyond the horizon. Join an organization (like CODEPINK!), start a book club, apply pressure on your representatives, engage in direct action, and never lose hope. Only together will we win. As Arundhati Roy said in 2002: “Another world is not only possible, she’s on her way. Maybe many of us won’t be here to greet her, but on a quiet day, if I listen very carefully, I can hear her breathing.”

articles.title: Inside the Epic Battle Over Control of a CA Grocery Union
articles.author: Chris Brooks
articles.content: Eric Marcuz is one of the most naturally gifted rank-and-file organizers I have ever met. Overflowing with passion for his union, love for his coworkers, and C4 Energy drinks, he has been spending what little time he has outside of working full time as a dairy clerk at a Safeway grocery store in Redding, California, driving for hours to visit grocery stores across the state and talk with his fellow union members. Marcuz is running for president of United Food and Commercial Workers (UFCW) Local 8–Golden State as part of the At What Cost slate, a group of seven rank-and-file grocery workers who are committed to giving their coworkers something that should be taken for granted: an opportunity to choose who leads their union. Standing in their way are staff supporters of Jacques Loveall, the local’s longtime president, whose family has maintained tight control over the union for more than four decades. Loveall inherited the presidency from his father, Jack, in 2004, through an appointment by the union’s executive board. Neither father nor son ever faced a contested election for the presidency, and the union’s top officers and executive board have been filled through appointments rather than competitive elections. The Lovealls seem straight out of central casting for a Hollywood depiction of out-of-touch, self-serving business unionists, complete with exorbitant salaries, palatial offices, a private jet, and even a bronze bust of the family patriarch. The At What Cost slate is fighting to introduce real democracy into their union. To do that, they must first collect hundreds of signatures from their fellow union members scattered across California. They have until November 17 to collect and deliver the required number of signatures. If they are successful, ballots will be mailed on November 21 and counted on December 7. The reformers have only the next few weeks during one of the grocery industry’s busiest times of year to campaign — if the union’s staff and leadership don’t stop them. The UFCW is one of the largest private sector unions in North America, representing more than a million workers, primarily in grocery stores, retail, meatpacking, and food processing. These are some of the lowest-paid and most exploited workers in the labor movement, but also some of the most indispensable to daily life, as the COVID-19 pandemic made painfully clear. Nearly everyone comes face-to-face with a grocery worker every week. This gives grocery workers a strategically important position in an increasingly concentrated industry where powerful corporations squeeze workers through understaffing, speedup, and automation while consumers struggle with rising grocery bills. Fights for democracy within megalocals — often the combination of multiple small union locals to create huge bodies that are difficult for rank-and-file workers to have real democratic say in, like UFCW Local 8 — have the potential to connect the fight for better wages and working conditions at companies like Albertsons, Kroger, Vons, Save Mart, and Safeway to the broader working-class struggle against runaway inequality. The stakes of this local election extend far beyond who will run the union. It raises the question of what kind of power tens of thousands of grocery workers could exercise if they were organized and mobilized to fight together. Which is why, after donating to their campaign, I traveled to California to spend a few days observing Marcuz and other slate members as they crisscrossed the state gathering signatures, visiting nearly twenty grocery stores in multiple towns and speaking with dozens of unionized grocery workers. I heard firsthand how grocery workers are being crushed by the rising cost of living and stagnating wages, how excited many are at the possibility of new union leadership, and how terrified some of them are of the union’s current leaders and staff. Dozens of workers described how union staff have been openly sharing their plans to harass and intimidate the At What Cost slate members as they try to gather signatures. Staff are also following behind At What Cost slate members and pressuring the workers they have spoken with into withdrawing their signatures to get them on the ballot, using a special form the staff have made specifically for this purpose. One grocery worker, who asked to remain anonymous out of fear of retaliation, described how union staff were openly discussing efforts to prevent Marcuz from qualifying for the ballot. Staff explained that if Marcuz failed to collect the required 443 signatures, there would be no contested election and Jacques Loveall would remain president. Staff were out doing everything they could to keep him from reaching that threshold. One produce clerk who has been a union member for over thirty years described Local 8’s well-known use of intimidation tactics to crush union democracy as “Jim Crow unionism.” He refused to sign Marcuz’s petition because he didn’t want “to end up in a ditch” for crossing staff. The heavy-handed intimidation tactics I’ve seen here are clearly having the intended effect on some union members. But for others, watching their own union’s staff try to stop a fellow worker from running for office has backfired. Ryan Crahm, a longtime Save Mart employee, said he wasn’t going to get involved until he saw four union staff representatives swarm Marcuz in his store. “It was straight up intimidation, and it made me pissed,” said Crahm. “I want to ask Jacques Loveall why he is so afraid to have someone run against him. And I want to know why it is that we never saw any staff reps before, but now that there might be an election, they’re in our stores all the time.” At What Cost Donning a baseball cap and a backpack filled with petitions, flyers, stickers, and homemade bandanas, the forty-three-year-old Marcuz is excited, urgent, and confident. Visiting store after store from 5 in the morning to 11 at night, he takes his time, listening, asking questions, and sharing his own experiences. His approach to petitioning resembles deep canvassing — a patient, open, and story-driven approach to sharing experiences while engaging with workers during a union drive or voters during an election campaign shown to be effective at winning hearts and changing minds — more than typical rapid-fire signature gathering. Few of his conversations run less than twenty minutes, and they typically cover a range of topics. Workers repeatedly open up to Marcuz about their frustration with the union contract’s pay scale and how the basic building blocks of the good life — home ownership, a reliable vehicle, vacations — feel increasingly out of reach. California fast food workers have a $20 minimum wage, but under Local 8’s contract, it takes members working full time about five years to reach that hourly rate. Since many grocery workers struggle to get full-time hours, it takes many of them seven or eight years, even in the delis and in-store Starbucks franchises, to earn what they could be making on their first day working at a neighboring In-N-Out Burger. Members also described unpredictable schedules, chronic understaffing, and the chaos caused by new artificial-intelligence-assisted inventory systems. Many were frustrated not only by the erosion of their contracts but also by how little say they had in negotiating them. There are no elected bargaining teams, and contracts are negotiated exclusively by the president and other appointed leaders and staff. Eric Marcuz speaks with a produce clerk at a Safeway in Lincoln, California. (Courtesy of Kelly McManus) Members, including several stewards, repeatedly complained about union staff who are rarely in the stores, don’t return phone calls, can’t answer questions about the contract, and are seemingly never around when members need them. The local’s website doesn’t provide information on the twenty-plus appointed vice presidents who allegedly represent members, or which staff representatives service their stores and how to contact them. The local also refuses to provide members with digital copies of their contracts. Remarkably, despite talking to dozens of union members, including more than a few who had worked in these stores for decades, I couldn’t find a single Local 8 member who had actually met Jacques Loveall. If the union was primarily known for anything, it is for its absence. “My mind was blown by how little visibility we had into our contracts, union negotiations, and the leadership’s decision making,” said Marcuz. “I started driving down to the union meetings in Sacramento. They’re two and a half hours from my house and held once a quarter at 8 at night. I went to my first meeting, and it literally lasted five minutes. I was the only member there.” Marcuz says he spoke up at a different meeting and asked whether, given the vast jurisdiction the local covers, quarterly meetings could rotate between different cities across the state to encourage more members to attend. He says the staff laughed him out of the room. So Marcuz started a petition, collecting three hundred signatures from grocery workers in his area demanding that the meetings at least be live streamed over Zoom so members could listen in. This time, he says, staff angrily shouted him out of the room. “Every time we tried to get involved, to make our union more responsive to the membership, we got smacked down. And once we start losing faith in our own union, we are on the road to no longer having one,” said Marcuz. The At What Cost slate is proposing sweeping changes in how the union functions. They want elected bargaining teams, open negotiations that members can attend, local meetings that encourage member participation, a $20 minimum wage in grocery, and aggressive contract campaigns backed by leadership that isn’t afraid to strike over ambitious demands. Marcuz and his small rebel army want to elect new officers, win better contracts, and fundamentally change who is exercising power inside their union, transforming members from mere spectators into active participants in the fight to better their working conditions and lives. Not a Union, but a Family Business The Loveall family has held tight control over UFCW Local 8–Golden State and its predecessor, UFCW Local 588, for more than four decades. Jack Loveall was first appointed president of the union in 1984 and ran it continuously until he retired in 2004, when his son Jacques was appointed by the union’s executive board to succeed him. At the time he retired, Jack Loveall was one of the highest-paid union officials in the country, making over $1 million a year in today’s money. The local owned a twin-engine business jet and had two pilots on staff to shuttle Loveall around the state. He oversaw the construction of a new union headquarters in Roseville, near his personal residence, which featured an 1,100-square-foot presidential office, the size of a modest house, complete with a sauna and marble wet bar. The local also paid $28,000 a year to cover the cost of Loveall’s membership in an exclusive Roseville country club, an expense the union president justified to the press by stressing that it was a place to talk business with employers. During his final year in office, there were seven Loveall family members on staff, comprising a quarter of the union’s payroll. Loveall built his empire through a series of mergers that expanded the union’s membership and assets while consolidating his control over its leadership. According to a 2004 investigation by the Contra Costa Times , critics accused Loveall of securing mergers by rewarding the officers of absorbed locals with lucrative positions in his administration. When Local 498, a Sacramento meatcutters’ union with 1,600 members and $2.3 million in assets, merged into Local 588, its former president saw his annual pay jump from roughly $12,500 to $85,000, while its former treasurer’s pay increased from less than $11,000 to nearly $76,000. The mergers helped Loveall build an increasingly loyal staff and executive board, with well-paid positions that extended to the relatives of some officers. But Loveall wasn’t always successful. Members of Local 1179 put a halt to a proposed merger with Local 588 by organizing an opposition campaign centered on Loveall’s pay and perks, arguing their dues would be better spent if their local remained independent rather than contributing to Loveall’s lavish lifestyle. Responding to these criticisms, Loveall told the press , “Just because we run a union doesn’t mean we’re supposed to be paupers” and said that “my members don’t want me driving around in a stagecoach or working in some shithouse office.” The elder Loveall also bragged about how tightly he controlled the union membership, saying that members were “ready to do what I tell them to do.” Jacques Loveall took over the top spot in 2004 but kept his father on the payroll earning more than $70,000 a year as a consultant, on top of his pension, until the elder Loveall died in 2020. Jacques is also chair of the Loveall Foundation for Children, a nonprofit founded in honor of his father and described on their website as being founded and run by “the staff, family and friends of UFCW 8–Golden State.” The union has financially supported the nonprofit for years, including $25,000 in 2025 alone, and at least one major collective bargaining agreement negotiated by Loveall obligates the employer to contribute three cents for every hour employees work directly to the Loveall Foundation. The salary of the president is set by the union’s top officers and vice presidents, all of whom were appointed over time by other top officers and vice presidents as vacancies arose. At no point over the past four decades have any of the Local’s top officers or the twenty-plus vice presidents actually been elected by union’s membership. Discussing this reality with other union members, Marcuz is blunt: “Our local hasn’t been acting like a union. It’s been run like a family business.” A Long History of Schemes and Intimidation There have been past attempts by union members to challenge the Lovealls’ tight control over the union. But those who have tried have repeatedly encountered a familiar combination of intimidation, interference, and mergers that postponed or eliminated the possibility of a contested election. Union activists in UFCW Local 1179 who were active in the effort to block the proposed merger with Local 588 reportedly experienced aggressive intimidation and surveillance from Loveall’s associates. According to an investigation by the Contra Costa Times , union staff began following reform activist Michael Ross-Smith, staking out his home and trailing him in union vehicles. In June 1994, three Local 588 business agents following Ross-Smith rear-ended his car in Walnut Creek, an incident documented in a police traffic collision report. A union representative acknowledged to the press that staff had been following Ross-Smith but defended the practice as a legitimate effort to investigate Loveall’s political opponents. In 1997, Raley’s grocery clerk Jack Nordby attempted to challenge Jack Loveall for the presidency. Nordby wanted to cut the excessive salaries of union officers and open contract negotiations to the membership. Following his announced run for office, Nordby alleges that union representatives followed him and his family, harassed him while he collected nomination signatures, and pressured workers into withdrawing their signatures from his petition. So many signatures were withdrawn that Nordby failed to qualify for the ballot. Another reformer, Lorna Greenlee, described similar intimidation. Greenlee said two union representatives confronted her while she collected signatures, then berated her for hours. She and her daughter also reported seeing union representatives watching their home. Although Greenlee said she had nearly collected enough signatures to run against Loveall, she eventually withdrew out of fear. The Lovealls have also benefited from mergers that postponed contested elections. In 2006, another reform slate, led by longtime meatcutter Doug Slaydon, was preparing to challenge Jacques Loveall. But before members could vote, Local 588 merged with Local 1288 to create UFCW Local 8–Golden State, postponing the election until 2008. Slaydon, who was fired from Safeway shortly after his attempted run for local union office, believed the merger was designed to prevent his challenge. Nearly two decades later, the same maneuvers again threatened to derail the current election. In October, Local 8 members received an election notice announcing that ballots would be mailed in November. But buried in the notice was a provision stating that the election would be canceled if the local completed a merger with an organization called Staffing Agencies Federated Employees (SAFE). None of the rank-and-file members of the At What Cost slate had ever heard of SAFE. The organization claimed to represent thousands of workers, but there was no evidence of where those workers were organized or what contracts SAFE had negotiated. What they did find were more connections to Loveall: a family member was listed as SAFE’s president on its initial federal filing just eight months before the election. The At What Cost slate, working with the UFCW reform organization Essential Workers for Democracy, on which Marcuz serves on the organizing committee, challenged the proposed merger and called for a Department of Labor investigation. After a federal investigator began asking questions, Local 8 announced that the merger had been postponed indefinitely, five days after it was announced. The election was back on. But that doesn’t mean the rank-and-file reformers would be allowed to campaign without interference. Fear and Intimidation on the Campaign Trail On November 2, Marcuz drove to the union’s headquarters in Roseville to pick up the nomination petitions that he and his slate needed to start collecting the hundreds of signatures required to qualify for the ballot. From there, he headed south toward Fresno to begin collecting signatures from grocery workers. But shortly after leaving the union headquarters, where a bronze bust of Jack Loveall stands in the central hallway, Marcuz noticed a black pickup truck following him. When he stopped for gas, the truck stopped too. He recognized the driver as Jeff Berns, a senior Local 8 staff representative whose brother, Mark Berns, was appointed by Jaques Loveall to chair the election. Multiple members of the Berns family have been on the local’s payroll going back decades. Mark Berns is currently the highest paid nonofficer staff member at the local, earning more than most of the vice presidents. He has repeatedly served as the local’s election chair, including in 2009, when the Department of Labor found that Local 8 had violated federal labor law by burying an election notice inside a union newsletter, mailed just a week after another issue with a nearly identical cover. The notice was so inconspicuous that members could easily have mistaken the second mailing for a duplicate and thrown it away without realizing an election was approaching. Despite finding that the local had violated federal labor law, because investigators couldn’t identify any member who said they would have run for office against Loveall, the department concluded that the violation had not affected the election’s outcome and took no further action. According to Marcuz, Jeff Berns told him that he intended to follow him throughout the day to make sure workers heard the Loveall team’s side of the election. And that’s exactly what he did. Berns followed Marcuz to a Save Mart in Fresno, where Marcuz and fellow slate member Mike Romero say three union representatives, including longtime Vice President John Micheletti, confronted them and interfered with their attempts to collect signatures. According to Marcuz, Berns threatened to invalidate every signature his slate collected. This behavior continued as Marcuz left Fresno and traveled to meet Silas Saldivar, a twenty-six-year UFCW member and head clerk, at the Safeway where he worked in Modesto. Marcuz became so concerned for his safety that he called Saldivar, and they agreed to instead meet at Saldivar’s house. I traveled with Marcuz to the Safeway in Modesto, where Saldivar recounted the story to me. “I walked outside into my driveway to meet Eric and saw Jeff Berns pull up in front of my house in his truck. John Micheletti parked in front of my neighbor’s house and then got out of his car and started walking toward us. I looked at Eric and said, ‘Dude, is this guy serious right now?’ Those two guys sat outside and watched my house for over an hour,” said Saldivar. “I didn’t feel safe. I still don’t, honestly.” While Saldivar was recounting this story to me, two union staff showed up at his Safeway. They kept their distance but made it clear that they were watching us. One pulled out his phone and began recording us. Marcuz estimated that he had been followed for seven hours and roughly three hundred miles on November 2. The following morning, he filed a police report alleging stalking and harassment. The intimidation hasn’t been limited to Marcuz and the other candidates. Less than a week later, Mike Denham, a Local 8 staff representative, showed up at the Perfect Union cannabis dispensary in Shasta Lake, California, where Marcuz had recently visited and received overwhelming support from members. Many workers were frustrated that they had never seen a copy of their union contract and couldn’t get one from the local. One supporter had asked Marcuz to leave a nomination petition so workers on other shifts could sign it, planning to return it to him later. According to multiple workers who asked to remain anonymous out of fear of retaliation from their union, Denham, the union staffer assigned to the dispensary, subsequently arrived and demanded that they either destroy the petition or turn it over to him so he could destroy it himself. According to several members, Denham repeatedly insisted that Marcuz had acted “illegally” by leaving the petition with workers at the store. When workers refused to turn it over, Denham eventually left in frustration. “It’s absolutely insane that our own union staff would come into our workplace to intimidate us to stop us from participating in our own union,” one worker told me. Federal labor law guarantees the right of union members to participate in democratic elections. The conduct of Local 8’s leadership and staff could have legal consequences. “The quantity and variety of the efforts by Loveall’s team are not only shocking, but likely unlawful, and could lead to the Department of Labor having to step in and rerun the election,” said Will Bloom, law professor at City University of New York and board member of the Association for Union Democracy. Discouraging Participation Is Anti-Union At a Vons grocery store in Fresno, multiple workers confessed to us that their union staff representative, Justin Putney, aggressively pressured them to sign the Loveall slate’s nomination petition. Workers told me Putney had forcefully instructed them to call him if Marcuz or anyone else from the At What Cost slate showed up so that he could come down and run them out of the store. It wasn’t long before that happened. Members working in the Starbucks kiosk were signing Marcuz’s petition when Putney came running up. “There he is,” Putney announced. “I wish I could say it was nice to meet you, but it isn’t.” Putney proceeded to lecture Marcuz about how “there is a right way and a wrong way to do things.” Putney, he said, had done things the right way. He had worked his way up through the union, starting as a steward before being appointed to a member advisory committee, then the executive board, and finally landing a position on staff. Putney failed to mention that his father is also a longtime paid executive board member in the union — a point Marcuz raised and Putney didn’t dispute. According to Putney, Marcuz, by contrast, was doing it wrong. “You’re like someone who has been playing rec league soccer saying he wants to jump into the big leagues and play professional soccer.” Marcuz responded that he believed democracy was the right way for members to decide who should lead their union. “And I don’t think you should have the right to run for a job that you have no qualifications for,” Putney shot back. Marcuz challenged Putney over the union’s bargaining record. “Our last contract was horrible,” Marcuz said. “It only provided a dollar raise for topped-out, high-seniority clerks. Nobody else got anything. We are barely able to survive on our wages. I can’t afford a house for my family. I can’t buy a truck. We can’t afford to shop in the stores where we work.” “You can’t show me anywhere in the country where grocery workers have a better contract,” Putney insisted. “Any contract that the membership fights for and wins together is better than one that is delivered from on high without our involvement,” Marcuz replied. “Members should be in the room when negotiating is happening. We should own the outcome.” I introduced myself as a journalist following Marcuz’s campaign and asked Putney why he had rushed down to the store to confront him. “He is a threat to the future of our members,” Putney told me. “It’s my job to protect the membership, and he represents a threat to that.” I asked whether he thought it was appropriate for union staff to confront members who were exercising their democratic rights, and whether he had been instructing workers to alert him whenever Marcuz showed up so he could interfere with his campaigning. “Yes,” Putney acknowledged. Marcuz was incredulous. “How am I supposed to exercise my rights if everywhere I go I’m being accosted by people on the union’s payroll?” he asked. “I have a right to speak with members, and you’re showing up here just to stop that from happening.” Putney maintained that he was simply encouraging workers to be cautious about what they signed. Marcuz wasn’t buying it. “Discouraging people from participating in the democratic process of a union election is anti-union. This process should strengthen us as a union, because it should cause the incumbent union leadership to state and defend their platform. We should debate our visions and what we are fighting for, and the members should get to vote on the best ideas,” said Marcuz. “But that is not what is happening. What’s happening is that I’m being followed, my conversations are being interrupted, and I’m being harassed by staff who have no honest interest in what I have to say and are only trying to stop others from hearing what I have to say. Let’s be honest. Your goal is to make sure that we don’t have a choice.” Putney denied the accusation, but Marcuz continued. “You tried to merge with a fake union that doesn’t really exist and that Jacques Loveall put his cousin in charge of. Staff followed me three hundred miles and sat in front of a member’s house for over an hour to try to intimidate me from participating. You have encouraged people in this store to report to you that I’m here so that you can come here and interfere with my campaigning,” he said. “None of these actions are to prove to the membership that your vision for our union is better. All of those actions are to prevent democracy in our union.” As the exchange continued, a crowd of grocery workers were gathering to listen. Eventually, a distraught-looking manager approached Putney and asked to speak with him privately. Marcuz took that as his cue. We left the store so he could continue gathering signatures, hoping that he wouldn’t be followed. “Solidarity Works” Loveall and the executive board members supporting him are running together on the “Solidarity Works Team” slate. And their materials look deceptively similar to official communications from the union. “Solidarity Works” has been Local 8’s slogan for at least fifteen years, appearing regularly in union communications, especially those concerning contract negotiations. Loveall himself has described it “as the motto of UFCW 8–Golden State.” A recent Solidarity Works Team mailer sent to every Local 8 union member’s personal address is virtually indistinguishable from an ordinary union communication. For one, the return address on the mailers is the union headquarters. For another, it features Loveall’s photograph and title as union president, invokes the local’s record of bargaining victories, and describes the Solidarity Works Team as a “network of member contacts” that lays “the groundwork for the solidarity, communication, and mobilization that will be needed when bargaining begins.” A QR code on the mailer links to the Solidarity Works Team website, where members are encouraged to join the team by providing their contact information. What the mailer and website don’t mention is that the Solidarity Works Team is running for reelection. There is no information on any of the slate’s candidates other than Loveall, and the word “election” doesn’t appear anywhere on the mailer or the slate’s website. The website is carefully crafted to lead members to believe they are signing up as part of the process of preparing for contract bargaining, not agreeing to receive information to vote in support of the current leadership in an election that isn’t mentioned anywhere. While out visiting stores, multiple grocery workers told me that the union staff representatives had asked them to update their contact information to prepare for upcoming negotiations. The representatives handed workers their phones and had them fill out a sign-up page, only for the workers to later discover it was to receive messages from the Solidarity Works Team slate. Those members subsequently received text messages notifying them that “petition signing is under way” and warning, “Reminder: DO NOT sign anything for anyone you don’t know. Solidarity Works!” The Loveall slate’s materials also issue stark warnings about “anti-union campaigns” and “attempts to weaken your bargaining power and possibly your benefits package.” In a video posted on the slate’s website, staff warn: “Be very careful with your signatures. Do not sign petitions. Do not sign cards. Do not trust the word of people who say they are with our union that you are not familiar with. Again, you should not be signing anything for anyone you do not know.” Anyone who has organized a union will recognize these talking points. They’re the same warnings employers routinely deploy during union-busting campaigns: beware of outsiders, don’t trust anyone asking for your signature, don’t believe their promises, and don’t risk the wages and benefits you already have. Only this time, these warnings aren’t coming from an employer but from the union’s own leadership. Jacques Lovall did not respond to an interview request for this story. “We Are at War” At a Safeway in Lincoln, a suburb outside Sacramento, I meet Mary MacDonnell, who has worked in the grocery industry for over thirty years and supports the At What Cost slate. The night before we met, John Micheletti arrived at her store and began badgering her and others to sign the Solidarity Works Team slate’s petition. Micheletti loudly announced to a group of members gathered near her that “we are at war. The union is under attack. That is why I am here.” The author interviewing Mary Macdonnell while being surveilled in the distance by a Loveall supporter. (Courtesy of Kelly McManus) MacDonnell has just finished her shift, and Marcuz and I are sitting on the bench outside the front entrance of the grocery store talking with her. She is emphatic that her union should be an organization of workers, run by workers, to fight for workers. That can’t happen if the union’s leadership is completely insulated from the membership and the staff and executive board are packed with relatives and appointed loyalists. She says she was drawn to the At What Cost slate because they practiced what they preached. The slate is encouraging members to talk and listen to each other, to build relationships, to be courageous and more ambitious, and to see greater member involvement as a source of strength for the union, not a threat to be mocked or ham-fistedly suppressed. As we are talking, one of the Loveall slate supporters from the night before arrives. He posts up with his back against the brick wall on the other side of the store’s entrance, conspicuously watching us. “This has been hella intimidating,” MacDonnell sighs as she eyes the man. But then her resolve seems to harden. “I respect Eric, but at the end of the day, this is bigger than any particular candidate. I want a choice. And I’m just not going to allow them to take that away from us.” This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. articles.title: Jesus' Message
articles.author: Peter Laarman
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Not so fast with the sheep and goats talk… As a longtime student of Bad Religion and its many manifestations, I tend to be on my guard when the New Testament gets into the news. When this happens, there is often something hinky going on. Matthew 25 recently made it all the way into the New York Times because of the number of politicians with winning midterm campaigns who are proud to call themselves “Matthew 25 Christians.” Had the Times reporter scratched a little deeper, she would have seen that the political deployment of this New Testament chapter, specifically its final section (vv. 31-46), is actually nothing new. Operatives for Barack Obama deployed it in 2008 ; and even before then, progressive evangelical Jim Wallis was calling Matthew 25 his “conversion chapter.” Eloquent Third Reconstruction advocate William Barber often cites this passage. So what exactly is my beef with this? Do I not find Christ’s condemnation of bad actors quite deeply satisfying? Actually, I have several concerns. To begin, church people of a bright pink persuasion (and yes, I am one) will always be wary of using proof texting for any purpose. Proof texting, as in claiming that “the Bible says…x, y, or z.” Some of my LGBTQ comrades used to call this poof texting because of the way certain Bible passages were used to clobber us. On account of these passages, Jim Wallis himself was very late to accept the idea that homosexuality is not actually condemned by God. Related: From Columbus to Christian Nationalism: Rev. Peter Laarman on Religion, Conquest, and the Politics of Domination Hence my caution about the triumphant embrace of Matthew 25’s oracle of judgment in order to crow that the other side is finally getting its comeuppance: crowing, in this case, that the racist, anti-immigrant, pro-rich Trumpers are on the wrong side of the judgment seat, whereas we—the winners, the good guys—are destined for everlasting bliss. In Jewish tradition, nobody is supposed to rejoice over the drowning of Pharoah’s army; these kvelling Christians could learn something from their Jewish elders. A second concern: the mandate to stand with and minister to “the least of these” is clearly something Jesus followers are expected to take seriously. I certainly have no quarrel with this mandate or even with the important idea that God judges nations for their behavior. But have Democrats as a whole, even Democrats like Barack Obama who use the Matthew 25 language, been especially consistent about standing with the lost and the least? Seems to me we have a case of cheap grace when politicians claim the righteous mantle for themselves and then fail to deliver the goods, which happens again and again in a system driven by opportunism. My third concern: if you want to bring the Jesus POV into politics, and specifically, if you want to invoke the Great Reversal (“the first shall be last, and the last shall be first”) and lift up a jubilee theology (i.e., cancel the debts, let the prisoners go free), there are plenty of effective ways to do this, using scripture, without going all eschatological on us. Suffice it to say, there is major eschatological entanglement in Matthew 25. The chapter is built into a longer section often called the Olivet Discourse and dealing with last things. In fact, the 24 th chapter, flowing uninterruptedly into ch. 25, belongs with like passages in Mark and Luke that fall under the rubric “Little Apocalypse” and that clearly echo the language of the Book of Revelations. To wit, the righteous will suffer persecution; they must persist, stand strong, and await their final deliverance. Related: Christian Fingerprints on Europe's New World Crimes There is no doubt that many early Christians lived on an eschatological edge. The Apostle Paul, for one, clearly believed that Christ’s return was imminent. But was Jesus of Nazareth, who died in 33 BCE, predicting the conquest of Judea, the destruction of the temple in 70 BCE, and Rome’s persecution of Jews and Christians alike? Serious scholars, notably Paula Frederickson and Bart D. Ehrman, find this extremely unlikely. They see much of the so-called Olivet Discourse as the work of later editors. More to the point, do today’s Matthew 25 Christians really buy into the whole Second Advent package? Are they seriously preparing for Christ’s imminent return in judgment? Do they truly cotton to the idea that a Cosmic Christ will sit on a white throne in order to condemn bad people to everlasting torment? Methinks they haven’t thought these matters through! And, as I say, there are many other and better ways to evoke the Jesus ethic by drawing on the words we know the historical Jesus actually spoke. Me, I’m more of an apocalypse now kind of guy. I think that I am the one who needs converting, each and every day. I believe that I am the one who needs to be accountable to Jesus for lifting up the poor and casting down the rich in whatever ways I can. But I will always be wary of judgment thrones. I will certainly never assume that other people are the ones deserving hellfire – or presume that I myself am walking the righteous path. Because if there are words we know for sure that Jesus actually spoke, those words are these: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged. For the judgment you give will be the judgment you get, and the measure you give will be the measure you get.” (Matthew 7:1-2) Faith and Reason

articles.title: Resistance Runs Deep
articles.author: Joe Simpson
articles.content: Resistance Runs Deep Lessons of Collective Action and Solidarity from the Underground Railroad At The Water’s Edge In the 1800s, the deep, dark currents of the Detroit River held both danger and deliverance. On the last stretch of a grueling journey, freedom seekers might find themselves at the water’s edge, hearts pounding with fear and anticipation. On the opposite shore lay Canada, where slavery had been abolished and a new life finally hovered within reach. No more stolen labor, stooping over crops sunup to sundown for enslavers’ profit. No more whipping posts and auction blocks and families ripped apart. For the first time, their humanity would be recognized by the law. public domain Info Info “I do not recollect of ever seeing my mother by the light of day. She was with me in the night. She would lie down with me, and get me to sleep, but long before I waked she was gone.” – Frederick Douglass Underground Railroad Leader, Abolitionist, Author, Orator, Formerly Enslaved Freedom Seeker The river became the bridge to the first breath of that new life. At this critical crossing, evading capture could mean clinging to a flimsy raft or rowboat, slipping stealthily aboard a ferry, or crawling through a secret tunnel like the one beneath the original Mariners’ Church. Precise timing and trusted lookouts were key, and that need mobilized communities in Detroit. The odds of even making it this far were low. Only a small fraction of freedom seekers across the country would ever reach their destination. Those brave enough to undertake the journey faced relentless danger and revenge, including branding, whipping and death. The system was designed to shatter their hope. The institutional power behind the slave trade was deeply entrenched. Wealthy interests depended on it. Fugitive Slave Acts protected it. Bounty hunters profited from it. In fact, despite some restrictions, slavery existed in Detroit until it was fully prohibited when Michigan was established as a state in 1837. Yet against those forces stood another kind of power: ordinary people with extraordinary courage, in places like Detroit. “The Negro slave, denied education, de-humanized, imprisoned on cruel plantations, knew that far to the north a land existed where a fugitive slave if he survived the horrors of the journey could find freedom. The legendary underground railroad started in the south and ended in Canada. The freedom road links us together.” – Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. Attribution: Michael Barera, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons Info Info Detroit Resists Detroit’s legacy of social justice began long before factories and freeways. It was alive and powerful here at the water’s edge, where geography had made Detroit a critical crossing, but people helped make it a bridge to liberty for more than 40,000 freedom seekers. As early as 1807, decades before the first physical railway in the area was built, the grassroots movement of the underground railroad was already proving the power of solidarity and collective action. That fighting spirit continues to define Detroit. As UAW members, we see its echoes in the unionizing of hundreds of thousands of autoworkers, the Walk to Freedom with Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr., and today’s fights for civil rights and the working class. “I am for civil rights as a matter of human decency, as a matter of common morality. But I am also for civil rights because I believe that freedom is an indivisible value.” – Walter Reuther UAW President 1946-70 Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture, Photographs and Prints Division, The New York Public Library. "The Road to Liberty; a Station on the Underground Railroad." The New York Public Library Digital Collections, 1857–1997, digitalcollections.nypl.org/items/a3b2f320-c62a-012f-e14b-58d385a7bc34 Info Info Citation: Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture, Photographs and Prints Division, The New York Public Library. "The Detroit River, at Detroit, Michigan, in 1850, the Favorite Place for Fugitives to Cross into Canada: From an Engraving in Possession of C. M. Burton, Esq., of Detroit." The New York Public Library Digital Collections, 1857–1997, digitalcollections.nypl.org/items/4025d0c0-c6f6-012f-e773-58d385a7bc34 Info Info “I plead guilty of having helped runaway slaves to get to Canada. I was obeying a higher law even than my country’s.” – Levi Gildersleeve Abolitionist While freedom seekers largely devised their own escapes, it was mostly free and formerly enslaved Black people who led the vital support efforts. In Detroit, Second Baptist Church sheltered thousands of freedom seekers within its walls, many of whom were ferried to safety by George DeBaptiste, a free Black business owner, in his steamboat disguised as a wood‑hauling vessel. Standing with them in solidarity were Indigenous allies, White abolitionists, Quakers, and others committed to liberation. The movement drew strength from people with different experiences and resources who aligned to outmaneuver a system built to crush resistance. Ingenuity showed up in crafty disguises, creative hiding spots like caskets and crates, skilled forgeries, and surreptitious horse swaps to throw off bloodhounds. Warnings and guidance might be delivered through coded songs and bird calls, satirical newspaper columns, artwork, and quilt patterns. Attribution: Andrew Jameson, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons Info Info “Our spirituals, now so widely admired around the world, were often codes. We sang of “heaven” that awaited us and the slave masters listened in innocence, not realizing that we were not speaking of the hereafter. Heaven was the word for Canada and the Negro sang of the hope that his escape on the underground railroad would carry him there.” – Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Solidarity Solidarity takes different forms as it steps between an oppressive system and those at its mercy. A hidden passage. A courtroom protest. A speaking circuit. An organizing drive for a first union contract. A strike line. In every space, it strengthens us. Solidarity begins when people face the same threat and choose to stand together against it. It runs even deeper when we recognize that another person’s freedom, safety, and equality are connected to our own humanity and our shared future. Freedom, as Walter Reuther said, is an indivisible value. That truth lay at the heart of the underground railroad movement. A Monumental Legacy Today, its history is remembered through a pair of Underground Railroad monuments facing one another across the Detroit River, symbolically recreating the bridge to freedom. Previous Previous Previous Next Next Next 1 2 3 4 5 Open image in lightbox: Gateway to Freedom Monument at the Detroit River 2 Open image in lightbox: Gateway to Freedom Monument at the Detroit River 2 Open image in lightbox: Gateway to Freedom Monument at the Detroit River 1 Open image in lightbox: Gateway to Freedom Monument at the Detroit River 1 Open image in lightbox: Gateway to Freedom Monument Plaque at the Detroit River Open image in lightbox: Gateway to Freedom Monument Plaque at the Detroit River Open image in lightbox: Canada's Tower of Freedom Open image in lightbox: Canada's Tower of Freedom Open image in lightbox: Underground Railroad Tower in Canada Open image in lightbox: Underground Railroad Tower in Canada “Thanks be to Heaven that I have got here at last: on yonder side of Detroit River, I was recognized as property; but on this side I am on free soil.” – A Newly Freed Person in Canada, 1846 On Detroit’s riverfront, in Hart Plaza, the Gateway to Freedom sculpture captures the hope and determination of a small group of freedom seekers, braced against the wind and the odds. Engraved quilt patterns recall the movement’s ingenuity and cooperation. Across the water and down a side street in Windsor, Ontario, the granite Tower of Freedom celebrates the journey’s end, with intricate carvings that evoke the overwhelming joy of being free at last. Its bronze eternal flame reminds us that the work never ends. The monuments honor the courage and actions of the freedom seekers who pursued their own liberation, the Black leaders who built the movement, and the allies who refused to accept injustice as inevitable. We are reminded that solidarity is a powerful force that crosses borders and challenges oppressive systems. We Are All Detroit There is no greater tragedy in our nation’s history than slavery, and from those who fought for freedom we inherit lessons that still speak to us today. The history of the Underground Railroad does not belong only to Detroit. It stretches south to Mexico and north to Canada, through swamps in Louisiana, alleys in Philadelphia, churches in Ohio, and every space where people chose courage over compliance. Through personal and collective acts of resistance, their actions pushed the nation into confronting its great moral failure. Collective action has long been a proven force against institutional power, and that principle still speaks to us today. It invites us to ask ourselves and each other, “What would happen if we treated every struggle for justice as a shared one?” The answer is not written yet, but every act of solidarity brings it closer.
