articles.title: Anwar Shaikh Gave Us an Emancipatory Economics
articles.author: Clara E. Mattei
articles.content: Writing about someone who has changed your life and to whom you owe so much is much more difficult than I would have thought. It is impossible to feel capable of delivering even a fraction of what it would take to fully honor the human and intellectual memory of Anwar Shaikh. I met Anwar at a moment of great intellectual insecurity for myself that he helped me overcome. Now, in front of this blank page, that insecurity is back. At the same time, this state of mind allows me to fully reconnect with the memories of our first encounters and the development of a mentorship and friendship that has deeply shaped me as a scholar and as a person. Grounding Theory in Historical Analysis It was 2015, and I was struggling to pursue the research for my economics PhD in Pisa, Italy. It had been a tough couple of years: after a five-year university degree in philosophy and history, the doctoral program had thrown me into hardcore economics courses. There were intense examinations in mathematics, econometrics, statistics, microeconomics, and game theory, which I had survived by studying nonstop and memorizing formulas that I would obsess over at night, half awake, half in my dreams. After so many examinations and so much peer pressure, it took me a while to find a subject I could feel passionate about. Economics, as my course textbooks presented it, was a dry, abstract discipline, all about technique and not much about intellectual stimulation. I felt demotivated and especially out of place. Was I ever going to be fit for this? I cared deeply about social justice and critique of the system — I read Karl Marx’s Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts and Karl Polanyi’s The Great Transformation — but none of it seemed to fit the current canon of scientificity. My supervisor, Giovanni Dosi, suggested I work on austerity, and I agreed, but I could not find an approach that was not so deeply economistic, focused only on debt and growth. Finally, while desperately roaming the library, I found an article on Fascist economics in 1920s Italy. I realized its deep affinity with contemporary economic policies in Europe, especially Italy. That day, I had a moment of awakening and decided to embark on archival research to trace the genesis of these policies in the thought of the economists who were advising Benito Mussolini. The research was challenging. I adhered to no specific methodological framework. To make sense of things, I realized I had to surpass the narrow limits of what history of economic thought, economic history, or economics meant for the profession. In my scholarly journey, I had found supportive mentors — Nicola Giocoli, Alessandro Nuvolari, and George Peden, for example — but there was clearly not much space for me in Italian academia, especially within economics. I was not doing enough of what economics was supposed to look like, but to maintain my motivation, I could not conform. This is when an email from Anwar changed my life forever. It read: “Dear Clara, I could not stop reading your paper once I started! It is excellent, and I hope you continue to pursue the parallels between the post-WWI rationale for austerity and the subsequent reincarnations in the 1980s and again now. Congratulations on a fine piece of work.” I remember gasping with happiness and a sense of recognition that I had never felt before. Really? A scholar like Anwar was taking my research seriously? And in an economics department? In his role as chair of the Economics Department at the New School for Social Research, Anwar was responding to an exploratory email I had sent just a week earlier, inquiring about a visiting scholar position. I had only recently discovered the existence of a department where Marxian economics was part of the canon, where economics seemed to be about substance as well as technique. In that email, I had attached a chapter of my dissertation, but I had no expectation whatsoever that Anwar was going to open the file. But he did, and from then on he would continue to make clear the importance of understanding the history of economic thought as integral to the analysis of capitalism itself. He wrote again inviting me both as a visiting scholar and to give a talk on my work to the department. That email exchange was a real turning point in my life’s journey. When I arrived in New York City in September 2015, I went to Anwar’s office hours. His wisdom and generosity were traits that struck me immediately. He was not teaching that semester, but I would stop by his office to get his feedback on some ideas. The week before my scheduled department talk, he told me: “You know, we are hiring, and you should apply.” The message was implicit: take this talk as an opportunity to showcase your work. At that point, I was exhilarated. The amount of adrenaline I felt leading up to that 4 p.m. Tuesday seminar was something I would never experience again. Anwar fought hard for the department to hire me. I only learned this after I had begun working as an assistant professor of economics at the New School. He believed in me so strongly. I still have a hard time understanding why and have never felt worthy of such high esteem. My dear colleague Ying Chen, whom the department hired at the same time as me, and I were both so lucky to have his support. We will miss those lunches, sharing different varieties of spicy Chinese food over conversations both fun and serious. A Life’s Mission In the summer of 2016, right before I moved to New York to start teaching, I helped organize a couple of stops for Anwar’s book launch in Italy. The stops were at the International University College of Turin and at my alma mater, the Sant’Anna School of Advanced Studies in Pisa. Anwar had just published his masterpiece , Capitalism: Competition, Conflict, Crises . There is one conversation with him I will remember forever: We were sitting at a café on the Po River, and he started telling me about the commitment and devotion it had taken him to produce his book. It had taken him over thirty years to completely reset the foundations of economics and the study of capitalism. He told me that escaping the traps of dominant economic theory was a sacrosanct mission to change the world, that deep study carried enormous transformational weight, and that it required sacrificing a lot of worldly distractions. He emphasized that he had supported me so strongly because he had seen potential in my research and in my devotion to it. He believed I could make a critical contribution to the study of capitalism and the political dimensions of economics. The connection between so-called pure economics and fascism that I was unveiling was for him key to unsettling some accepted truths about our economic system. It was then that I promised him I would persevere. And in times of demotivation, his words are always there to motivate me. I spent another six years developing my book, The Capital Order . I always wondered whether the final result lived up to his expectations, but luckily, he did seem proud. It was really thanks to Anwar’s influence and mentorship that I was able to give a sturdy theoretical foundation to the archival research, tracing its roots in the deep tendencies of our economic system. I also wanted the archival research to bolster the systemic analysis, especially of the deeply political forces that shape our economy. More generally, the book is the product of the intellectual milieu of the department Anwar introduced me to. The intellectual stimulation and methodological insights I received, including from colleagues like Duncan Foley, completely transformed it. I remember the long conversations on the phone with Anwar during the COVID-19 lockdown, in which he meticulously commented on my interpretation of Ralph Hawtrey’s theory of inflation and explained how best to measure rates of exploitation and profit. His comments, often critical, were not easily digestible, and I would take them bit by bit and dissect them with Aditya Singh, my loyal research assistant, who was also Anwar’s student. Neither the Perfect Nor the Imperfect but the Real What Anwar has gifted us all is his formidable lens through which to interpret capitalism and challenge the mainstream. He offered a lucidity about the systemic tendencies of our economic system and a holistic approach that, as many, including Vivek Chibber , have already stated, bears comparison with that of Karl Marx himself. In my years working at the New School, I attended two of Anwar’s graduate courses. I experienced firsthand how he was able to translate the titanic amount of knowledge in his book into effective pedagogical tools. His story of the chicken pot pie, for example, embodies his capacity to convey the nature of capitalism in an intuitive and lasting way. Once Mary sold her chicken pot pie hobby to a business, it did not matter what was in the pies, which became full of hormone-treated chicken; what mattered was their price. With an image that stuck, Anwar explained the fundamental logic of value as being completely detached from use value, from those qualities that made the chicken pot pie so good. Anwar delivered, like no one else, the antibodies against bourgeois economics, against those “theories” that only help hide rather than explain. In his book, as in his classes, students learned to wear different lenses through which to look at the economic world. They came to understand the slick capacity of the “perfectionist” and “imperfectionist” approaches to idealize markets, competition, and progress. Shifting from one framework to another, examining their explanations of inflation, profits, and unemployment and their policy implications, Anwar was able to deliver a scathing critique of both neoclassical (perfectionist) and Keynesian (imperfectionist) economics. He tore down the edifice not just of neoclassical economics but also of its supposed Keynesian alternative with grace and precision. He unmasked how they shared much more than one would think, especially a common backbone of idealization and an urge to get back to perfection, which Keynesians thought state intervention could achieve. As he put it in his brilliant interview with the Institute for New Economic Thinking: “The notion of imperfection is a dual of perfection; you can’t speak of imperfection unless you are implicitly paying allegiance to perfection, and I do not want to be trapped in that space.” He also recalled something I had felt deeply myself: “When I started as a graduate student, I was surprised to discover that the representation of the world was an idealized fictitious form that makes no sense to me, and that as an economist you had to accept that, then spend your time showing how the world is imperfect.” That is why his blackboard did not have just these two possibilities: next to the perfectionist and the imperfectionist, there was a third column that had vastly more explanatory power. Anwar was not content with merely modifying the existing framework but spent thirty years rebuilding the foundations of economics from scratch. What he built was revelatory. And it had to start from real observation, from confronting the naked reality of capitalism. Real economics, he liked to call it: an approach that vindicated and expanded, both theoretically and empirically, the most important intuitions of Adam Smith’s, David Ricardo’s, and especially Marx’s analysis, without calling it Marxist. In this, Anwar was adamant and would not accept compromises. He thought it important to get out of the niche, to avoid the self-sectarianism typical of heterodox economists. As a matter of fact, he disliked the term “heterodox” for exactly that same reason: identifying yourself as an antithesis to the orthodoxy weakens the capacity of real economics to stand on its own feet and gain hegemony. As he wrote in the introduction to his book: “Its object of investigation is neither the perfect nor the imperfect but the real.” Profit as the Engine Anwar’s whole economic edifice rested on one crucial intuition that, paradoxically, the perfectionist and imperfectionist paradigms had disregarded: profit drives all the system’s dynamics; it is the engine of the whole economic system. The incessant quest for profits drives investment and economic growth. Profit shapes supply (firms produce with the goal of making a profit) and aggregate demand (purchases of inputs, plant, and equipment, and the hiring of workers and their capacity to consume). As he put it concisely in the slides he shared with me: “The profit motive always remains central, and its dominance creates the force field that shapes and channels microeconomic and macroeconomic outcomes. This is the proper meaning of the invisible hand.” He reappropriated the meaning of Smith’s invisible hand not as a metaphysical myth of the eternal efficiency of the market but as the expression of those profit imperatives that operated through real competition. Through the lens of the profit motive, Anwar drew a few fundamental intuitions. First, class struggle is at the heart of the system, and technological dynamism is one of its expressions. Modern economic analysis reduces capital to durable wealth and understands profit as a reward for abstinence and entrepreneurial search. Against this, Anwar reminded us that capital had nothing to do with the qualities of the commodity. Instead, it had everything to do with capitalism’s specific historical process — potentially infinite accumulation — and the class strugglethat grounds it. Indeed, profit mirrors surplus labor, and as he says, the existence of surplus labor is a “social outcome.” He writes: “Surplus product only arises when the length of the working day exceeds the working time to reproduce the standard of living of the employed worker, that is, only when surplus labor is performed.” Technological progress is no proof of the fairy tale that capitalism exists to maximize consumer satisfaction with ever better commodities. To the contrary, firms invest in new technology to squeeze more surplus out of their workers and to cut costs below their rivals’. In real competition, firms that fail to do so don’t survive. Second, the real rests on a conflictual structure, precisely the one that neoclassical economists seek to erase in favor of a harmonious scheme that persuades us to believe we live in the best of all possible worlds. Far from the “ballet” of perfect competition, it is a war of all against all. The business literature showcased extremely well how the profit motive played out through real competition. In Anwar’s words, “Firms set prices; they try to survive; some win; some don’t; they use tools to attack each other. Roughly 70 percent of firms die within the first three years.” As Chibber has pointedly discussed , this theory led Anwar to deconstruct traditional leftist understandings of the dysfunctions of capitalism. Capitalism’s violent outcomes do not stem from monopoly power “corrupting” competition; they arise precisely out of a system working as it should, driven solely by the quest for profit. Third, crisis is the norm under capitalism, an expression of crucial recurrent patterns or “gravitational tendencies” that emerge out of the very dominance of the profit motive itself. As Anwar put it, “The history of market systems reveals recurrent patterns of booms and busts over centuries, emanating precisely from the developed world.” These include the great depressions of the 1840s, the Long Depression of 1873–1896, the Great Depression of the 1930s, the stagflation crises of the 1970s, and the great global crises of the 2010s. In this long-run perspective, excessive financialization was merely the trigger of the 2008 crash; its underlying cause was a crisis of profitability. Anwar’s real economic framework can also explain other devastating features of our economic system, including the structural economic plunder of the Global South and permanent warfare as a stimulus to profitability that does not risk subordinating the profit motive to social goals. Such subordination is correctly seen as a threat to the capitalist order and labeled “socialistic.” My work on austerity’s structural role in managing capitalism — by repressing wages and preserving the social relations underpinning profitability — is charged by this theoretical insight. Indeed, it underscores how capitalist governments must find the “right” stimulus policies — those that do not challenge market dependence or the command of private investment. Turbulent Gravitation These observations are important to avoid easy misunderstandings. Anwar was not a determinist. The patterns he discovered were important to guide systemic knowledge but did not eliminate agency. Rather, Anwar developed a multidimensional structure of influence that is at once hierarchical and deeply historical. This is the significance of turbulent gravitation : a relatively small set of operative principles can explain a great variety of economic phenomena, without reducing the dynamics of capitalism to mechanical laws. There are observable patterns in the system — but humans can organize and change the system through political action. This is the deeply historical and political approach that runs through Anwar’s analysis. He repudiated the bourgeois distinction between, on the one hand, “ahistorical laws” and, on the other, the “contingencies” of history. One must understand that classes, through their historical agency, create the very imperatives upon which they act, even as those imperatives bind them. This is particularly important when it comes to the “gain-seeking behavior” that defines capitalism as a particular social form. The imperatives of profitability are not simply external laws bearing down on historical actors, nor are they merely the outcome of individual choices. Class relations and competition produce them historically, even as they confront those actors as real constraints that shape their actions. The beauty of Anwar’s economic analysis is that he could identify the underlying regularities of capitalism without abstracting them from the historical relations of class and agency through which actors continually reproduce them. This also speaks to Anwar’s particular relationship to empirical data. He was emphatically empirical, but not a positivist. His argument was that classical assumptions are consistent with empirical reality. He understood that data are never innocent. Data are not simply a collection of preexisting facts waiting for an observer. As he writes, “Theory intervenes not merely in the interpretation of events but in their very representation (and occasionally in their suppression, as we know only too well).” His example of unemployment is particularly telling: the official definition counts someone as employed if they did any work at all for pay or profit. Such a definition masks a much bleaker picture of the realities of unemployment and underemployment as structural features of the system. Anwar’s historical proclivity, expressed in his attention to social relations, is particularly clear in his passion for Michał Kalecki’s famous 1943 article, “Political Aspects of Full Employment,” which we discussed at length on many occasions. He thought this was one of the most important pieces of political economy ever written, as it clearly stressed one of the strongest Marxian intuitions: capital not only produces unemployment — it fundamentally depends on it. Keynesian economics, with its utopian delirium of ignoring exploitation, had depoliticized the economy. It failed to realize that its goal — full employment — was technically possible, but that only a fascist dictatorship could achieve it without undermining capitalism. Indeed, only under fascism can you forgo the impersonal discipline of unemployment because political discipline is firmly in place. I draw heavily on these conversations in my most recent book, Escape From Capitalism . Anwar reviewed it in detail and wrote a final blurb for it: “A book for the times. Mattei takes aim at the notion that the forces which regulate market and social outcomes are socially neutral. Mattei argues that we need to reject this framework, to ‘politicize our lives to participate in the transformation of the material and social reality around us’ at the local and global level.” Anwar’s approach deeply inspired the book, and I try to bring it to life for a broader, nonacademic audience. I carry forward his conviction that economics is a social science and therefore a historical and political science. I especially carry forward what I understand to be the fundamental Shaikhian spirit: it is only by explaining how capitalism really works that we can sharpen our tools to overcome it. Indeed, Anwar’s work has inspired generations of young people and won international acclaim. “Don’t Give It Up” Anwar was extremely supportive of my embarking on the journey to the University of Tulsa. He gave a brilliant opening lecture at the inaugural conference of the Center for Heterodox Economics there, which I had organized. He remained deeply supportive throughout the turbulent times at the university and when I began setting up the independent Forum for Real Economic Emancipation (FREE). I helped organize a wonderful retirement celebration for Anwar, which produced a special issue on his work in The New School Economic Review . Afterward Anwar enjoyed his new home at the lake in Amherst, writing, fishing, cooking, and visiting friends like Robert Pollin. We spoke on the phone often. Anwar had helped create the intellectual ethos of the New School for Social Research Economics Department and had opposed academic hierarchies all his life. He was appalled at the administration’s attacks , like firing tenured and untenured faculty members and blocking PhD admissions, which were effectively dismantling the department. His recorded words at the retirement party ring true to all of us: The important thing about democracy is that you have a voice. It does not mean you have to agree with me. You have to have a voice, and you constantly need to protect it, and you have to act on it. Look around you — no department anywhere has this kind of voice. So don’t give it up. No matter what they do. They are going to try to make you give it up. Don’t give it up. Go and strike if you have to. Close the place down. Carrying the Work Forward Iremember the shock of that phone call in which he told me he had cancer. I pretended it wasn’t real: his voice was so combative that it seemed impossible that anything could beat him. To the very end, as he heroically fought his devastating illness, he remained focused on his scholarship and on the possibility of delivering an abbreviated version of his masterpiece, updated with new empirical data. Anwar’s archives at Bard College reveal letters that Joan Robinson and Nicholas Kaldor wrote to him in the 1970s, already recognizing the power of his work. Fortunately, Anwar leaves behind a considerable number of students, now spread across the world. A recent piece by Nikos Chatzarakis perfectly exemplifies their power to speak of his breakthroughs. As his former student Juan Santarcángelo, now a professor in Argentina, has forcefully put it, “Anwar will never truly die; he will live on in each of us and in those who were lucky enough to know him.” It is our task to carry his paradigm forward, advance it, and spread it widely, publishing and making his work available in many different forms. This is something to which I intend to devote considerable energy in the coming years. Anwar was one of the most powerful thinkers of our time. His legacy finds an especially important place in this historical moment, when the violence of capitalism is rampant and the thirst for radical political change so strong. The massive archive that his youngest student, Nicholas Anderson, has digitized, now held at Bard College, is a treasure that we need to cultivate and explore in detail. It is Anwar’s real economics, and its potential for full emancipation, that we need to keep alive as a guide to collective action and the possibility of change. This is what we are trying to do at FREE , an assembly-based project for empowering education and concrete postcapitalist alternatives that is spreading globally. I hope many more people will join us in this collective endeavor for a humane, profit-liberated future. articles.title: The Executioner and the Loyalist: How Harvard Spent Summer 2026 Gutting Its Largest Union for Financial Gain
articles.author: Working Mass: The Massachusetts DSA Labor Outlet
articles.content: A sign held up at the joint HGSU-HAW strike picket line in November 2026, referencing sister union HUCTW’s culling months before (Working Mass) By: Tony A, Adrian Aliano CAMBRIDGE – With the first strike by their workers that year abated, and two other unions’ anger rising, Harvard executives spent the summer of 2026 carrying out far-reaching cuts that gutted the ranks of the largest union on campus: the Harvard Union of Clerical and Technical Workers (HUCTW). In the end, hundreds of people were kicked out of the halls of the university to which they dedicated their lives, just for Harvard leaders to report exorbitant earnings made off their backs only weeks later. The decimation required an executioner and a loyalist, but started with a secretive firm: McKinsey & Company. Leaders in the Faculty of Arts and Sciences (FAS) appointed a task force to address “Workforce Planning” on April 24, 2025. Under their oversight, Harvard University started paying McKinsey & Company in quiet installments starting August 2025. Harvard paid McKinsey a total of $250,000 for FAS consultation. In other words, Harvard hired a firm that not only has contracted with ICE, but where whistleblowers report consultants become “functionally the equivalent of full-time ICE employees” when working for ICE, rather than protect their international students facing deportation from that same agency. Sinister change crept into Harvard within months of the final installment. Hiring the Executioner Warren Petrofsky was at Cornell University when workforce planning at Harvard FAS began. As Associate Dean of Administration from 2023 until his departure in 2026, Petrofsky “helped shape long-term strategic vision and resource allocation for $4000M enterprise,” as he proclaims on LinkedIn. Part of his Cornell tenure included the signing of an agreement with the Trump Administration for money: $60 million, as well as compliance with the federal government’s definitions and orders regarding civil rights definitions. Beyond big deals with bigger devils, according to Cornell Sun reporting, the College of Arts and Sciences at Cornell cut $11 million after “very specific” funding guidelines sent to every department by Petrofsky. He developed a reputation, before his hiring, as the man who would comb through every line and cut any position – ruthlessly. Petrofsky completed his undergraduate education at the University of Pennsylvania and spent a combined over two decades at Penn working in computing and operations. In that time, he completed a Master of Business Administration (MBA) at Wharton before his promotion to Chief Infrastructure Office for the School of Arts and Sciences. That position was charged with saving Penn money, the role he took on at Cornell. Harvard scooped Petrofsky from Ithaca within one fiscal quarter of the University’s last quiet installment to McKinsey & Company. Warren Petrofsky was appointed Dean of Administration and Finance of the Faculty of Arts and Sciences on April 20, 2025: in short, he became Harvard’s money guy, apparently strategically identified following his work saving two other Ivy League universities money. The University’s press release cited his previous experiences in “administrative transformation within complex, decentralized Arts and Sciences environments,” like Cornell. Though Harvard recognized Petrofsky’s role at Penn in the same breath as that at Cornell, Working Mass has not been able to verify if he was responsible for extreme cost-cutting at the expense of others at Penn. How much Harvard University currently pays Warren Petrofsky is unknown. While his role at three consecutive institutions may have been cutting costs, the cost to human beings be damned, Petrofsky could not complete his work without cutting workers. There was one problem: the workers had a union. “You Can’t Eat Prestige” The Harvard Union of Clerical and Technical Workers (HUCTW), the largest labor union on campus, was founded and built through hardwon battles with executives holding the same anti-labor position as the current administration. The union has a memorable slogan: “You can’t eat prestige.” HUCTW represents over 5000 rank-and-file support staffers distributed across the Harvard University system; in every office, laboratory, library, clinic, theatre, museum, and facility their work is evident. The union is the largest labor union on campus and among the oldest in Harvard Yard. Harvard University never wanted to recognize HUCTW. The 1988 NLRB ratification was the culmination of a seventeen-year long struggle. As then-union director Kris Rondeau said to the audience, “their unmistakable goal was to beat the union, and they just failed.” Organizing HUCTW had begun but ultimately failed before reaching a majority of support twice before, both starting in Longwood, but the third attempt in the mid-1980s was successful. A small core organizing committee of Medical Area workers grew the union to win the support of the over-4000 staff members across the Harvard apparatus. The union started independently, without affiliation with the United Auto Workers (UAW) or other internationals. Eventually, HUCTW affiliated with AFSCME Local 3650 in 1987, the year before winning NLRB recognition. Harvard fought with anti-union talking points and booklets strategically distributed to supervisors across the ranks, as well as hostage meetings about why workers should not support unionization, right up till its loss. The democratic vote was not seen as legitimate by Harvard executives. After HUCTW members won the battle for legal representation and the right to collectively bargain in 1988, Harvard still fought against recognition by appealing to the National Labor Relations Board. Harvard tried to get the union election result thrown out by arguing HUCTW coerced workers to join. Harvard saw its case thrown out instead. September HUCTW rally in Harvard Square (Working Mass) Someone Has to Do It? Decisions are made by individual people in power. Harvard did not unconsciously, as a detached force, hire Petrofsky to do the institution’s dirty work. Just like the decision to pay a firm that whistleblowers describe as “morally bankrupt,” people made the decision to hire him. Some are on boards; others are bureaucrats. Hoekstra rose behind Claudine Gay to take over as the Dean of the Faculty of Arts and Sciences when the latter became president of Harvard University in August 2023 – right before Harvard’s hard turn right, the cutting down of Gay, and the ascent of health economist Alan Garber from within the bureaucracy’s top ranks to the presidency in January 2024 by convenient accident . In November 2025, Hoekstra described in a financial update the central need to “reduce our structural deficit through lasting, mission-aligned change.” Her next update followed that winter: the hiring of Warren Petrofsky. On February 27, Hoekstra announced Petrofsky’s appointment by lauding his pivotal work at Cornell University and the University of Pennsylvania, including “helping guide one of the institution’s most consequential operational efforts” at Cornell – an apparent allusion to Petrofsky’s pivotal role in culling that $11 million in Ithaca. “Disciplined financial stewardship,” advised by McKinsey & Company, required finding cuts in the Yard. Sometimes, hired Yes Men say the truths their bosses hide. Answering to Hopi Hoekstra directly, Deming blabbered in one April 2026 open forum that many “back office” jobs doing “things you would never really know or care about, frankly… are the first places I’m looking to try to save money.” The rank-and-file got the message: they were on the chopping block. The institution they built decided they were excess to trim. HUCTW leaders countered in an April 29 email obtained by Working Mass: Would it be invisible to students if their tuition payments were delayed or mishandled because staffing was slashed? Would it be invisible to researchers and students if their labs could not function because materials were not ordered, payments to vendors were not processed, or equipment was not repaired? Would it be invisible to the University if admissions, financial aid, course enrollment, or fundraising—all of which sustain access to education—were disrupted due to large staffing cuts? The implied threat was largely ignored. When contract time arrived, HUCTW leaders negotiated a tentative modest agreement and wrote a strongly worded email to Dean Deming and FAS administrators, as HGSU’s strike continued in the rush towards the end of the semester. Hundreds of union members expressed misgivings with union leaders’ approach. When the contract ratification vote took place in May 2026, the final tally counted at 3074 in favor and 767 opposed – the largest nay vote in union history. The administration seemed to have no other methods to cost-save except culling worker ranks. Deming spouted vague musings on “new ways to do things” more economically, like renegotiating contracts with outside vendors to alleviate some of the burden of the University’s financial crisis. Executives also showed a knack for effective financial planning when Deming said , with characteristic nuance: We’re looking under the couch cushions for quarters. But while the University has been successful in exchanging people for dollars, many key contract negotiations have seen no success at all. Instead, Deming and the University’s record has, so far, been characterized by historic incompetence. Harvard has been unsuccessful in negotiating a single union contract this fall. Three different unions – HGSU, HAW, and UNITE HERE Local 26 – have since authorized strikes. On July 22, the act was complete: hundreds without jobs, within 90 days of Petrofsky’s start date. As hundreds of workers were removed and members of three unions representing other parts of the workforce driven closer to strike action, the Harvard endowment grew by $11 billion between the 2025 (~57 billion) and 2026 (~68 billion) annual reports. The loyalist had turned around her institution’s deficit by casting the workers who built the institution out into the cold. She made a deal with the man who made deals with devils. Her job, whether “mission-aligned” or not, was a success. In a bed afforded by her near ~$700,000 annual salary, Hopi Hoekstra could sleep at night with job safety surrounded by supporters ready to reassure her she did her best. Few others had that luxury. September HUCTW rally in Harvard Square (Working Mass) When a Tenth of Your Colleagues Vanish Among the rank-and-file, where executive decisions are felt in debts and rents, one Harvard staffer learned over Zoom that Harvard eliminated their job while waiting on the runway for takeoff. Nearly 15 months of instability crawled by as workers waited for Petrofsky, Hoekstra, and their ilk to decide the impact of hundreds of lives. Finally, on July 22, 2026, an email obtained by Working Mass dropped: “before any individual conversation takes place, all College staff will hear from FAS HR with the information and guidance they need.” That guidance would ultimately prove misleading. With five minutes remaining till the end of day, impacted Harvard staffers received calendar invites from FAS HR inviting them to meetings the next day, without consideration for their own schedules. Staffers were informed that while they did not need to change their plans, they were still expected to “take the meeting by phone if Zoom is not feasible.” Despite their active membership in HUCTW, one rank-and-file worker that spoke with Working Mass reported that HR originally discussed the severance package for non-union staff with them. Only after the employee requested clarification of benefits for HUCTW members did the HR representative recognize their error and place importance on the contractual and legal obligations of the institution they represented. Working Mass was unable to identify how many rank-and-file workers were similarly misclassified. The mix-up is representative of some of the reported dysfunction at Harvard’s latest round of layoffs. The “reorganization plan” laid off both union and non-union workers and left remaining staff to perform workloads previously managed by multiple employees without additional compensation. The cutting especially of HUCTW members whose work was essential also placed major incentives on bosses at the University to ask graduate workers and academic workers to take on more work to make up for the gaps their colleagues left behind. These reported workload increases further incentivized workers to strike this fall. Harvard eliminated 10% of its workforce, including 165 staff positions in FAS, before culling positions across the social sciences in a total of a third of its staff fired, after 2025 cuts of student advisors: 75 workers , in all. As part of this rollout, Deming unveiled the dismantling of the Office of Student Services (OSS) and the merging and effective closing of multiple other departments serving undergraduate students. Each closure meant workers either out of work or with more work or both. “It’s been really hard,” bemoaned David Deming, whose position remains integral to cutting others, this week. Based on his sound understanding of the available evidence, he surmised: “I think staff feel stretched. They feel a lot is being asked of them, and I know that they know that.” The workers more than knew how much executives were squeezing them. Blood and “Reorganization” Cuts were justified under a broader reorganization effort to consolidate administrators and departments. In the Financial Overview of the Financial Report for the 2026 Fiscal Year , Treasurer Timothy Barakett addressed the culling of staff ranks: Achieving a surplus demanded an extraordinary amount from this community… to colleagues directly affected by these changes, we owe more than gratitude: our respect, and our recognition of all they contributed to Harvard. One Harvard employee countered, quoting the HUCTW slogan: Just like prestige, laid off workers can’t eat respect; and recognition for our contributions, as they cut our jobs anyway, offers the same impact as the calories in tap water. About 24% of impacted employees were offered the opportunity to reapply to similar positions. This mechanism took advantage of contract language: since the positions were technically new roles, Harvard management was able to add more responsibilities without added pay. Other elements of the “reorganization” that dramatically increased workloads were previously described in the leaked McKinsey proposed model verified as instituted by Working Mass, such as multi-unit administration. Instead of individual department administrators, which values long-term commitment and service, Harvard has consolidated multiple responsibilities from multiple departments into a handful of positions. These, in turn, answer to a smaller group. Essentially, under the consultation of McKinsey, the structure and power therein is more centralized into fewer and fewer hands. At a rally organized by the HUCTW Rank-and-File Movement in Harvard Square in September, members shared their stories: laid off after 35 years of service, cut during parental leave, just a few examples of Harvard’s perfidy toward their own workers. Other members, some with 25 years of employment, announced that they were forced to take demotions under the restructuring despite recent glowing performance evaluations. Membership cited personal distress after the potential for layoffs was announced in the Fall of 2025, and subsequent emotional impacts of the extended period of uncertainty. “The inability to plan has been really hard for me and a lot of my colleagues,” one worker said. In accordance with the “WARN” Act , both union and non-union members received 60 days’ written notice in advance of their mass layoff date. One HUCTW member told Working Mass that impacted rank-and-file workers had access to the Work Security Program which, according to their website, “provides members with full pay and benefits—typically for five months, but possibly up to eight months—after layoff notification, as well as job search support, while members look for a new position.” While additional benefits were associated with union membership, even some members expressed dismay over one significant problem: non-union colleagues were not afforded the same. ‘In a back room’ The HUCTW website outlines that “Harvard is required to negotiate with the union before finalizing any plans, to provide information around the basis for any proposed changes, and to allow for the development and discussion of alternative proposals to prevent job loss.” However, during this process, staffers did not have the ability to directly engage in open bargaining or any form of negotiations participation that felt democratic. Instead, HUCTW leadership and management hashed out a “backroom deal” before reporting back to the membership after the fact. Bill Jaeger, long-time staff organizer and originally a rank-and-file member during the 1980s HUCTW organizing drive, made an unusual move for a staff member: he attempted to sway membership, in the face of the largest resistance yet mustered by the HUCTW Rank-and-File Movement to a meagre contract. In an email obtained by Working Mass, Jaeger argued that members should approve the contract because HUCTW’s modest gains were bigger than other campus unions readying for strike action: The raise we’ve arrived at for 2026 is a solid one – it beats inflation from the past 12 months and it’s a stronger increase than other Harvard employee groups have seen for this year. Bill Jaeger left HUCTW after several decades of service following contract ratification. 20% of membership ended up voting No (767 members), which was 301 more than the previous ratification vote. HUCTW rank-and-file members that spoke with Working Mass said unionwide meetings prior to the layoffs mostly walk through the handbook and processes. Some members are concerned that HUCTW leaders are not doing enough to push back against cuts. “It’s not about making changes or listening to input,” one employee said. In mid-August, HUCTW leadership sent an email to membership outlining the state of the FAS Layoffs, Reorganization, and Hybrid Work, claiming: HUCTW leaders were able to save many staff from layoffs and provide others with more options than they would otherwise have, but ultimately FAS administrators are still moving forward with significant number of job elimination. They reiterated that during the Layoff Consultation Process, they “insist that administrators seriously consider every available alternative to job loss.” The words felt feeble even to many members. One laid-off worker said: Insistence for serious considerations of alternatives to job loss feels a lot like the hopes and prayers of placating politicians. Union leaders and reformers must surely grapple with HUCTW’s responsibility to its community and membership, beyond the narrow sectional interests enshrined in contracts negotiated behind closed doors. That’s particularly true when three other unions of colleagues have aligned their action to maximize its impact on Harvard, while HUCTW remains on the sidelines. But it is Harvard executives, with names like Petrofsky and Hoekstra, who have earned the ire of labor – and labor does not forget. Can Warren Petrofsky sit easily knowing the children and children’s children from multiple institutions will curse his name, just like his actions, as the fiscal executioner he chose to become? Can Hopi Hoekstra sleep at night for the rest of her life knowing the rest of the lives of hundreds of colleagues, even their ability to stay home and housed, have been forever shaped by her decision? Can administrators walk across Harvard Yard comfortably knowing their legacies are that of monsters? Tony A and Adrian Aliano are associate reporters for Working Mass. articles.title: The Scandal of Flávio Bolsonaro’s Escape Won’t Fade Away
articles.author: Felipe Antunes de Oliveira
articles.content: To exfiltrate means “to smuggle [an intelligence agent, soldier, etc.] out of an area under enemy control.” The term belongs to military jargon, rather than to political commentary. Nevertheless, the Brazilian media has been using it to describe the sudden removal of former presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro from Brazil’s territory a couple of days after he lost the second round of this year’s presidential elections. José Roberto de Toledo, a veteran journalist, was probably the first to use the word “exfiltration” in relation to Flávio Bolsonaro, in his influential weekly podcast . The circumstances of Bolsonaro’s escape seem to come directly out of a spy film. Smuggled in the middle of the night across the border with the active participation of a former Mossad agent and US government officials, he reappeared in Florida and pledged to take the details of his escape to his grave. An exfiltration is not an act of political sympathy. It is an extremely risky operation to preserve an asset from being captured by the enemy. On the one hand, the exfiltrated asset enjoys safety when he finally reaches his destination; on the other, the exfiltration makes all masks fall, and the fugitive’s true allegiances become transparent. For that reason, if Flávio Bolsonaro was indeed exfiltrated to the United States, this episode should figure side by side with the kidnapping of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro as a blatant example of US neo-imperialism in Latin America. The political and legal responsibilities for this case cannot be brushed under the carpet of history and will certainly come back to haunt Brazil-US relations for decades to come. A Very Suspicious Escape The details of Flávio Bolsonaro’s escape from Brazil are not entirely known. So far, The New York Times has reported that Jason Miller, a White House operative, arranged the luxury private jet that Bolsonaro and his family used (at the cost of almost one million reais , paid for by an American corporate account). The party crossed the border with Argentina through means that are not yet entirely clear, most likely by land, on the night of Tuesday, October 27, near Foz do Iguaçu. Brazil’s top Sunday night TV news show, Fantástico , revealed that a former Israeli intelligence operative accompanied the fleeing Bolsonaro family. From the Argentinian border location of Puerto Iguazú, the disgraced former presidential candidate took a private jet to the United States, stopping in Ecuador for refueling and avoiding Brazilian airspace. Arriving in the US, Flávio Bolsonaro landed at the infamous Miami–Opa Locka Executive Airport, used six decades earlier to prepare for the US-supported Bay of Pigs invasion of Cuba, one of the worst historical examples of direct US imperial aggression in Latin America. Upon arrival, despite presenting his canceled diplomatic passport, Bolsonaro received “ parole status ” and was escorted by a motorcade to an undisclosed location. Who Takes Responsibility? Donald Trump’s secretary of state, Marco Rubio, was quick to deflect responsibility. “ We didn’t facilitate anything,”claimed Rubio in a press conference on the sidelines of a G20 meeting a few days after the fact. He knew that confessing the exfiltration would mean exposing the State Department to serious internal and international reckoning. Flávio Bolsonaro himself told The New York Times he would take the details of his fleeing “to the grave.” In an open letter released after his arrival in the United States, he compared himself to figures like José Martí and Charles de Gaulle and denounced the election result. He also thanked Argentine President Javier Milei “for his courage, sense of justice, and legality” and expressed his gratitude to Trump “and the wonderful American people” for hosting him. By fleeing Brazilian justice, Flávio Bolsonaro has secured protection, at least for now, from having to answer for his alleged crimes in two different investigations. More important, as long as he is safe in the United States, it becomes more difficult for Brazilian investigators to prove the precise nature of his ties to Washington. He is not the first person to have claimed US protection in suspicious circumstances. His younger brother Eduardo has been agitating from Texas for the Trump administration to impose sanctions against his own country, while the former head of the Brazilian intelligence agency under Jair Bolsonaro is also on US soil, having dodged immigration enforcement under very mysterious circumstances. However, Trump and Rubio cannot shield Flávio Bolsonaro from justice and history indefinitely. It took decades for Washington’s involvement in military coups across Latin America in the 1960s and 1970s to be proven with overwhelming evidence. A comprehensive apology is yet to materialize. Hopefully, we will not need to wait that long this time. A newly elected Democratic-controlled Congress should hold US officials accountable for any interference in the Brazilian democratic process. It should clarify whether US taxpayers’ money was used to facilitate Bolsonaro’s escape from justice and whether he promised his eventual US handlers any specific information or advantages, beyond his public pledges to give the US preferred access to Brazilian rare earths . In due course, Flávio Bolsonaro must be extradited, and cables and intelligence documents pertaining to this case should be declassified, so that the Brazilian and American people can finally learn what really happened on the night of October 27. articles.title: The Dominican Government Uses Zionism to Whitewash Trujillo
articles.author: Simón Rodríguez
articles.content: On August 24, the Dominican government announced its adherence to the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance’s (IHRA) definition of antisemitism. President Luis Abinader , a businessman of Lebanese descent, made the announcement at the opening ceremony of the Sixth Latin American Forum Against Antisemitism,held in Santo Domingo by the US-based Combat Antisemitism Movement (CAM). Abinader also promised to invest 50 million pesos (approximately US$852,000) in the construction of a Jewish museum in Sosúa, in the north of the country, where 747 European Jewish refugees settled during the 1940s. The foreign ministry statement announcing Abinader’s decision included a defense of the Trujillo dictatorship (1930–1961) as a supposed opponent of discrimination, hatred, and religious intolerance. Rafael Trujillo, whose dictatorship was fanatically racist, perpetrated a genocide against the Haitian population along the Dominican border between late 1937 and early 1938 and was obsessed with “whitening” the Dominican Republic, whose overwhelming majority was and continues to be of African descent. The government’s invocation of Trujillo’s legacy is key to understanding its real motivation in pledging allegiance to the IHRA definition of antisemitism. The Dominican government is an unconditional ally of Israel’s apartheid regime. One of its first measures upon coming to power was a statement in 2020 in favor of establishing the Dominican embassy in Jerusalem. In 2023, the Santo Domingo International Book Fair had the Israeli embassy as guest of honor. An agreement with Mekorot, Israel’s state-owned water company, to design a national water management plan was signed, and there is also Israeli cooperation with the Dominican office for the technification of irrigation. President Abinader has drawn inspiration from the Israeli wall system that encloses Gaza and Palestinian communities in the West Bank for his own border wall with Haiti, and he has relied on the purchase of Israeli weapons to drive the largest arms buildup in the country since the Trujillo dictatorship. The government also relies on Israeli technologies for internal repression, having used Pegasus spyware against a journalist who was investigating corruption. The current Dominican government’s claim to oppose discrimination runs counter to all evidence. It has refused to introduce legislation against hate crimes and incitement to racial or religious hatred. The Penal Code, which took effect in August 2026, defines the crime of discrimination but effectively eliminates any penalty for discriminatory actions justified on religious grounds or in which the legitimate exercise of a legal authority is invoked, which amounts to the legalization of discrimination. The 1943 law banning the Vodou religion, enacted by Trujillo, remains in effect and is used to persecute Afro-Dominicans and Haitians. Meanwhile, a 1962 law prohibiting the glorification of Trujillo and Trujilloism is not enforced. Neofascist paramilitary groups that praise Trujillo, Benito Mussolini, and Adolf Hitler operate openly and collaborate with the police to repress the Left and Haitian communities. In this context, Abinader, like Trujillo, claims to oppose antisemitism in order to whitewash and further his own racist agenda. In Service of Genocide CAM, which promoted the Dominican adoption of the IHRA working definition of antisemitism, is linked to the Israeli foreign ministry. Both its CEO, Sacha Roytman-Dratwa, and its editor in chief, Barney Breen-Portnoy, have worked in communications for the Israel Defense Forces. Senior Israeli officials , such as the country’s current president, Isaac Herzog, have served on its advisory board. The organization has promoted the criminalization of the slogan “From the river to the sea, Palestine will be free,” following the example of the Austrian government in 2023. The Jewish Council of Australia has considered CAM’s summits on antisemitism to be part of an effort to silence criticism of Israel’s genocide against the Palestinian people by equating it with antisemitism. In its statements, CAM has defended Israel’s military actions in Gaza, describing them as an exercise in self-defense . Conversely, the International Association of Genocide Scholars has described Israel’s actions and policies in Gaza as crimes against humanity and war crimes and has stated that they meet the legal definition of genocide. Among the organizations that initially affiliated with CAM was the Clarion Project , an anti-Islam lobby that has been classified by the Southern Poverty Law Center as a hate group. For the Dominican government, hosting a CAM event and adhering to the IHRA definition serves four main purposes: it reaffirms its political subservience to US foreign policy, contributes to whitewashing the image of its ally Israel, portrays the Dominican regime as opposed to discrimination, and attempts to rewrite history to present the Trujillo dictatorship as the initiator of an alleged antidiscrimination policy upheld today by Abinader. There is indeed continuity between the Trujillo dictatorship and the current regime, but in a different sense. One Hand Washes the Other The statement from the Dominican foreign ministry announcing the adoption of the IHRA definition of antisemitism asserts that “the Dominican Republic underscores its ongoing commitment to the fight against all forms of hatred, discrimination, and religious intolerance, a position it has consistently maintained since 1938, when the Dominican state was the only one to offer asylum in Sosúa to a significant number of Jewish refugees.” The Dominican government goes on to urge all governments to take measures to “prevent hatred, intolerance, and discrimination in all their manifestations.” These are curious statements in light of Dominican history, not least the last six years of rule by Abinader’s right-wing Modern Revolutionary Party. That the Dominican government considers itself the heir to the Trujillo legacy is an important admission. President Abinader , named in the Pandora Papers leaks for having offshore accounts, has also admitted to sharing the ideas of dictator Joaquín Balaguer, who ruled the country with an iron fist from 1966 to 1978 and before that was one of the main ideologues and officials of the Trujillo regime. Since 2021, Abinader has been enforcing an undeclared state of exception to carry out mass deportations of Haitians, including the systematic use of arbitrary detentions based on racial profiling, raids without warrants, and militarization of hospitals and their use as immigration detention centers, as well as widespread violence by migration agents, including murders, torture, forced disappearances, and sexual violence. articles.title: Heading to Congress, Will Lawrence Still Has Some Questions
articles.author: Liza Featherstone
articles.content: Will Lawrence has been part of every anti-oligarchic organizing effort that has mattered over the last two decades: Barack Obama–era climate activism, Occupy Wall Street, Sunrise Movement, housing justice, the Bernie Sanders campaigns, the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), and resistance to artificial intelligence data centers. Before the recent midterm election, the thirty-six-year-old East Lansing, Michigan native was exactly the sort of candidate who, according to conventional wisdom, could maybe beat establishment Democrats in liberal blue districts but would lack traction against the Right in a general election. Yet on Election Day, Lawrence proved that conventional wisdom wrong. He flipped a Republican seat in Mid Michigan and is now headed to Congress. Lawrence is not the only one showing that an anti-oligarchy, pro-working-class politics can succeed in purple and red America. From Maine to Montana, Bernie Sanders–style politics beat Trumpism across the nation. In Washington, DC’s incoming Congress, Lawrence, reached by phone while walking through the tunnels of Capitol Hill, joins numerous “regular people, many of whom are complete outsiders,” newly taking their place in Congress. They’re not just “regular” in the sense of not being billionaires. They’re also not career politicians. They “owe nothing to anybody” in power, Lawrence emphasizes, and they “have a mandate to root out corruption, get money out of politics, deliver economic security for their constituents, stop stupid wars, and stabilize the climate.” But Lawrence has serious questions about what’s possible in this moment. “We can undo everything that Trump has done,” he vows. “We can undo the Big Beautiful Bill. We can restore SNAP [the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program], Medicaid, and the ACA. We can take action to lower prices in certain sectors,” he says: And yet, economic volatility will continue. People will continue to feel that the future is looking worse. And we’ll still be stuck with the questions of, “What is America’s global role in the twenty-first century? How do we deal with the billionaires, the oligarchs, at the commanding heights of the economy?” He pauses, aware that he’s brought down the mood. I feel a bit superficial bringing us back to the elections, asking how he won his congressional seat, but it turns out not to be a change of subject or tone. Lawrence’s refusal of sunny platitudes continues. “Acknowledging the despair and disillusionment that people feel as rational and legitimate, and then drawing on those who have come before, to remember that people have dealt with adversity, uncertainty, and volatility and have fought back against the powerful of their time to win the rights and freedoms and quality of life that we have until recently enjoyed,” is crucial, he says. “The social compact of the New Deal era was fought for and won with blood.” Lawrence’s parents, like my own, worked at Michigan State University, and I’ve spent a lot of time in his hometown, a land grant university town bordered by flat cornfields on one side and Lansing, the state capitol, on the other. I’m not surprised his bleak honesty and capacious politics could draw Michiganders together. Lawrence unseated Republican incumbent Tom Barrett, a Trumper who staunchly supported the war in Iran and opposed extending the Affordable Care Act (ACA) tax credits at the beginning of this year. The district backed Donald Trump in 2024 but has flipped so often that it is regarded as a bellwether for the presidential election. “There are a lot of bad people,” Lawrence continues, and a lot of reasons to feel disillusioned when bad people manipulate their way into having a lot of power. And yet we have it inside of us to become the better versions of ourselves, to build a better version of our society. [The campaign] was all about that: giving people a reason for hope, creating space for community, for people to make friends and get to know each other, challenge each other, challenge themselves to take action and to take responsibility. “And it did,” he allows, passing the hopium pipe for just a second, “make me feel more optimistic about democracy. There is some juice left.” Lawrence isn’t calling himself a socialist these days. He let his DSA membership lapse, which he announced during the campaign, wanting to focus, he told CNN at the time, on uniting the district. He said that he wanted his constituents to feel he represented and was listening to them, rather than any specific organization. William Lawrence photographed in 2026. (Sabio117 / CCO 1.0 Universal ) Whether he was wearing his green-and-white Spartans hat at the tailgating parties on Michigan State’s massive campus, where the student vote shapes elections more than it does anywhere else in the nation; or canvassing or conducting town halls across the district, in small cities and towns like Grand Ledge and Brighton — this approach clearly resonated, winning over independent voters and even Republicans. “The more I continued with the campaign,” he tells Jacobin , “the more I just chafed at some of the attempts to label me as ‘socialist,’ ‘communist,’ or whatever, in a way that was about making people fear me.” So he decided, “Let’s just focus on the values and the issues. When we start there, there’s tons of common ground.” As he points out, he’s not alone among the incoming left wing of the party in taking this approach. While the new Congress includes New York City socialists Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier , it also includes Lawrence’s fellow Michigander, incoming Senator Abdul El-Sayed , who beat a Republican with a Bernie Sanders platform and no “socialist” label; or Troy Jackson in Maine, who did the same. “With this incoming freshman class that is large and historic,” Lawrence says, “people identify themselves in a variety of ways: progressive, moderate, none of the above. But everybody campaigned on the same issues. And they feel a mandate to deliver change.” It has been striking to see the continuity, across the country, of Sanders-style issues in the winning candidates’ platforms: Medicare for All, taxing the rich, childcare, defunding the war machine, a moratorium on AI data centers. It is a mandate against billionaires and for the common good. And, Lawrence suggests, there may be a variety of ways to express that: For the self-identified Left, my push is not to get too hung up on labels or making assumptions about others based on their labels. . . . The project of reconstituting the social and political compact for the twenty-first century has to be based in the bid for a supermajority of the people of this country. And there is no supermajority of this country who currently identifies with any common label. So, we have to be willing to listen beyond that and then find new symbols and perhaps new labels that allow us to establish that majority. Lawrence feels strongly about changing the direction of foreign policy, and this incoming class has a mandate to do that, probably for the first time this century. But he’s very worried about whether it can be done — and not for the reasons I’m expecting, like the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) and defense lobbyists. “For me, this is one of the lessons of Joe Biden’s administration, which I do really believe tried to do something good for the American working class and wanted to deliver on economic security,” yet was “so militarist and hawkish.” He points to the administration’s position on Israel and Palestine: “It completely undid the coalition that Bernie and Biden supporters had painstakingly built together for the sake of building a united front to defeat Trump.” Lawrence is worried about whether, in America, we can have peacetime social democracy. “Social democracy without a Cold War posture is unproven,” he says. “Social democracy was forged in the context of the Cold War. And in the attempt to reforge a social democracy [today], there will be those, like in the Biden administration, who believe that a new Cold War is a natural part of that project.” He’s right: During the Cold War, workers’ material gains — including civil rights for black Americans — could often be framed as part of an anti-communist argument that capitalism could deliver a better life for the working class than communism. And a state of permanent war readiness fueled the economy, bringing billions of federal dollars into defense spending and creating millions of good jobs. Lawrence worries that many Democrats still can’t separate militarism and social democracy, that they believe that ongoing war can “clarify the resolve and the sense of national purpose, but also that it’s the only way that we can have an economy which is prosperous, with a broad-based growth that includes a strong deal for the working class.” That won’t cut it today, he says: “I don’t believe that that will work for the twenty-first century, because the conditions of the political economy are different. It’s not 1946 anymore. And we’re not going to recreate the economic conditions that existed then. So we have to find a different way.” One of the fights that politically shaped Lawrence, a Sunrise activist, was the campaign for the Green New Deal during the Biden administration; it seems possible that an energy transition off fossil fuels could contain the seeds of that “different way.” Maybe in Congress, Lawrence can help bring those ideas back to political life. Maybe. But he’s certainly not overpromising. It’s jarring to talk to a politician who has thought so deeply about the perils and limitations of our moment and speaks so frankly about them. Not only does Lawrence not think perpetual geopolitical conflict can deliver for Americans. (Americans, squeezed by gas prices during the war in Iran, seem to agree.) “I really don’t want to see World War III. It’s as likely as not that that’s where things are headed,” he warns. “Preventing that is one of my main missions.” This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture.
